answers.question: J5-05: May a `thread_shared` value take its memory from an arena or other manager?
answers.program:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)               # a one-thread arena
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using level             # the list of types `using` may follow names `thread_shared`
    with scope = thread.scope():
        scope.spawn(owns fn() owns stats: stats.hits.fetch_add(1))   # the owner goes to a task on another thread
    println("done")                                       # the last owner ended on that thread, giving the block back to `level` there
answers.today: It compiles: TYP-46 (p04 433-434) and ALC-1 (p09 185-186) both list `thread_shared`. How it runs is not defined. `using` binds tighter than `thread_shared` (GRM-43, p03 435-438), so the `Stats` object is made in `level`, and its own block, the arena's memory, becomes the block that holds its counts (HEAP-3, p09 60-62). Every count change asks which thread made it, and OBJ-1 (p08 69-71) reads that from the header of the runtime memory chunk the block lies in. Arena memory has no such header, so whatever bytes are there are read as the making thread. Two threads may then both use the plain home count (RC-4 point 1, p08 159-162), a data race on the count. Since an Arena frees nothing one by one (ARN-2, p09 107-111), the value keeps no instance word (ALC-1 (1), p09 206-209), so LT-4's `sharedref mut` link does not come into it.
answers.after: E2114 at the line `stats = thread_shared Stats() using level`: "`stats` is shared between threads, so its block comes from the built-in manager, which records the thread that made it; remove `using level`". Written `stats = thread_shared Stats()` (with the now unused `level` line removed), it compiles and prints done. The task's end of the last owner is RC-4 point 4's at-once end.

decisions.title: Where the block of a value shared between threads comes from
decisions.problem: TYP-46 and ALC-1 let `using` follow `thread_shared`, but OBJ-1 finds a `thread_shared` value's making thread only in the header of the runtime memory chunk its block lies in, written when the chunk is made, never in the value. A memory manager's memory has no such header. So `thread_shared Stats() using level` has no making thread. The compiler cannot work out which thread runs a making line, so what remains is a refusal or a run-time mechanism.

|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main thread | `thread_shared Stats() using level` puts the shared object, its counts included, in the arena's memory | allowed by the spec today |
| 2 | any thread changing an owner count | asks which thread made the object, read from the header of the runtime memory chunk the object lies in | the arena's memory has no such header |

B: allow it for a manager with one instance that every thread may use (the platform's `System`), keeping the making thread in the object's 4 spare header bytes; refuse an arena.
C: allow the same managers as B, with the runtime taking its 64 KiB chunks (making thread in their header) from that manager instead of the built-in one; refuse an arena.

Outcome: decided_by_parameters. The making thread of a block a manager gave is a run-time fact with no chunk header to read it from, so the choices are a refusal (A), an id in the object (B) or chunks taken from the manager (C). A breaks no verdict; B departs from verdict 101 fix 1 ("never from the value"); C is a new runtime piece. A is the finder's recommendation, reached here by the parameters.

What the finder's reading missed:
- `using` binds tighter than `thread_shared` (GRM-43), so in the example it is the class object's own block, from the arena, that would hold the counts (HEAP-3).

- Where a manager does keep the word, verdict 164 already refuses making the value `thread_shared` through THR-1 (E7015).

from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)               # a one-thread arena

answers.today: On paper it compiles: TYP-46 (p04 433-434) and ALC-1 (p09 185-186) list `thread_shared` among the types `using` may follow. But OBJ-1 (p08 69-71) reads the making thread only from the header of the memory chunk the block came from, and a block from `level` has no such header. Moving the owner into the task's capture is a hand-over (RC-4 point 4), so the last owner ends on the task's thread and gives the block back to the one-thread arena there. No rule says how the counts or the end run, so the behaviour is undefined. In C++ terms: `std::allocate_shared` from a one-thread `std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource`, with the last `shared_ptr` released on a worker thread.

decisions.title: A thread_shared value's block always comes from the built-in manager
decisions.problem: TYP-46 and ALC-1 allow `using` after `thread_shared`. But a thread_shared value's making thread is read only from the header of the built-in manager's memory chunk, never from the value (OBJ-1, verdict 101 fix 1), and a block from any other manager has no such header. The value may also end on any thread (RC-4 points 3 and 4). The compiler cannot work out at compile time which thread made a block, so only a run-time record, a different counting scheme or a refusal remain.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. A keeps every thread_shared value on the measured two-count path (speed), is safe, and leaves the ordinary program unchanged. B and C each make these values slower: B reads the maker from the object (13% to 44% slower cross-thread copying, measured), and C uses one atomic count (it loses the measured 25% for a thread's own objects). 2. Safety. All three are safe, and A turns undefined behaviour into a refusal at the line. 3. Compile time first. A is decided when compiling. B or C would be needed only if refusing lost a correct program, and none is lost: the value's meaning (shared between threads) stays without `using`, and what it holds can still come from any manager its fields' types name. With a one-thread arena, only scoped tasks can reach the value anyway (LT-4), and a plain view does that. 4. A written word only for meaning. A removes a word that cannot do what it says, and adds nothing to write. 5. The ordinary program is unchanged. 6. Consistency. There is one way to find the making thread (OBJ-1, verdict 101 fix 1) and no second header path (checklist 13), and the refusal at the making line matches verdict 165.
decisions.recommendation: A. It keeps verdict 101's single way to find a shared object's making thread, makes the mistake a refusal at its line, and costs no program anything it needs.

owner_short.today: The spec allows `using` after `thread_shared`, but the only way it gives to find a shared object's making thread needs the built-in manager's memory, so such a program has no defined behaviour.
options: A: refuse `using` on a thread-shared object; its memory always comes from the built-in manager (what it holds can still come from any manager).
B: allow a manager that has one instance and that any thread may use; the object stores its making thread in its own header (a second way, and cross-thread copying of it measured 13% to 44% slower).
C: allow such a manager; the object is counted with one atomic count from birth (a second counting path, slower on its own thread).

holes.today: `Global` is the package's configured allocator, here TALLY (ALC-2 p09 224-227; ALC-3 p09 237-239). RT-1 (p18 243-246) says allocation is the system malloc per block, and a host may supply its own allocator (FFI-27 p16 685-688). OBJ-1 (p08 69-71) reads the making thread from 'the header of the memory chunk its block came from'. No rule says a block TALLY hands out lies in such a chunk, so how the counts and the end run is unspecified. In C++ terms: a biased refcount reading a garbage owner id.
holes.with_edit: The same. The edit's added words 'only the built-in manager's chunks carry that header' now assert something no rule makes true for a configured or host allocator.
holes.what_goes_wrong: If the runtime takes each thread_shared block straight from `TALLY.allocate`, there is no record of the making thread. Two threads may both count as the making thread, which means a race on the home count and a double end. This happens with or without the edit; the edit's soundness argument rests on the missing rule.
holes.fix_hint: State that the runtime keeps every thread_shared block in chunks it makes and records itself, whatever allocator the package or host supplies.

Verdict: the edit decides J5-05 safely. The property it states (a thread_shared value's own block always comes from the built-in manager) is right and costs nothing. It is broken by one medium hole of its own words (hole 1).

The refusal on the making line is worded by position: "`using` after `thread_shared` ... on the line that makes the value". GRM-43 binds `using` to the value just before it, and TYP-46 says what a value holds is decided by its fields' types. So that wording can refuse correct programs whose `using` names a field's or a list's memory: a level with its mesh in a frame arena, or a batch list of shared jobs in a level arena. outs.notes:
Verdict: broken = true because of hole 1 (medium, caused by this edit). The choice itself (A: a thread_shared value's block always comes from the built-in manager) holds up under the engineering lens. It keeps verdict 101's one way to find the making thread, nothing runs for it, it adds nothing to write, and the ordinary program is unchanged. Every program in the answer and its siblings decides as the edit states.

What is wrong is the wording's trigger. The refusal is keyed to word order ('`using` after `thread_shared`, in a type or on the line that makes the value'), not to the property its own first sentence states. In a type this agrees with GRM-3 ('`using` applies to the whole type before it'). On a making line, GRM-43 (p03 435-438) and p06 108-109 make `thread_shared [..] using m` a list whose own memory comes from `m`, and HEAP-3 / p10 328 then put the shared block in the built-in manager. So the edit refuses a correct `using System` list with a message that is untrue for it, while the same layout written as a class field (its own AssetCache sibling) compiles. A repair keyed to 'the block that carries the header' fixes this without growing.

That repair changes how the Parser sibling (one-thread FixedArena list) is refused: it becomes E7015 by verdict 164 (the list's LT-4 instance link may not reach another thread) instead of E2114. The spec text of THR-8/THR-9 (p11 43-68) does not yet list `sharedref mut` among the non-Send kinds, so verdict 164 has to be in the text for that.

Hole 2 is filed as pre_existing. The edit's 'every place' claim for class objects holds only if `thread_shared` before a call's result is E7017 (THR-1 p11 71-72, 'on a value made otherwise'), not 'a new value' (OWN-13 p07 139-140 with BRW-12 p07 200-201). The spec reads both ways today. If the lead takes the second reading, hole 2 becomes a hole of this edit.

Holes 3 and 4 are low. Hole 4 asks only that A's per-value allocation cost against an arena bump be stated (to measure).

Hole 5 (OBJ-1's chunk header against RT-1, ALC-3 and FFI-27) is pre-existing. The edit's reason rests on it, and its to_verify already lists the runtime check.

Also pre-existing, not filed as a hole: a type cannot say 'a shared list whose elements come from manager M' (GRM-3 against GRM-43 for `shares` and `thread_shared` collections).

The edit's follow-ups (p17a 83, p17 641) are confirmed. Appendix I rows for TYP-46 and ALC-1 do not quote the list.

Read-only throughout. Nothing was run. One `sed -n`/`cut` was used to read a long table row. docs/AUTOPILOT.md and HANDOFF.md were skipped as the workflow instructs for review agents.

out.intent: Count hits on one Stats object that main and a task share, with its memory taken from a one-thread arena, then print done.

existing_rule.words: Which thread made a value is read from the header of the memory chunk its block came from, written once when the chunk is made, never from the value.

edits.before: `owns`, `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` type
edits.after: `owns`, `shares` or `shares mut` type
edits.why_general: In a type, `using` applies to the whole type before it (GRM-3, p03 189-190: "`owns Mesh using LevelArena` is an `owns Mesh` whose block comes from a `LevelArena`"). So after `thread_shared T` it always names the block that holds the value's header, which the next sentence refuses. The entry comes off the list so that the list and that sentence never disagree. A `thread_shared fn()` type, which has no such header, then gets the general E2114, as a plain `fn()` does.

edits.before: `E2114` ("an `int` has no memory of its own to take from `LevelArena`; remove `using`").
edits.after: No `using` names the block that holds a `thread_shared` value's header: the thread that made the value is read from the memory chunk that block came from (`[OBJ-1]`), and only a block the runtime takes for a value made with no `using` lies in such a chunk. So `thread_shared Stats using System` and `thread_shared Stats() using level` are `E2114` too ("`stats` is shared between threads, so its memory comes from Ember itself, which records the thread that made it; remove `using level`").
edits.why_general: The property is about one block, not about where words stand. It is the block that holds a counted `thread_shared` value's 32-byte header, and the making thread is read from that block's chunk. These words reach every `using` that names that block. In a type: a field, a parameter, a result, or generic code over `A: needs Allocator` (GRM-3). On a making line: a class object made `thread_shared` (HEAP-3: it "already has its block") and a struct that the word puts in a block. They reach every kind of manager the same way: an arena, a pool, `FoundByAddress`, `System`, and `Global`, which is a call to the configured allocator (ALC-2 p09 224-225), not the runtime's chunk path. They do not reach a `using` that names some other block. That covers a list's own buffer (`thread_shared [..] using frame`, which GRM-43 binds to the list, decided by Send and ThreadShared as `new_in(frame)` is), a field's memory, a list of shared values made in an arena, and a function type, which has no such header. TYP-46's existing sentence "what it holds comes from where its own fields' types say" still decides those. The two examples show the type form and the making-line form, and nothing is added per case. The exception gives its reason, as principle 6 asks.

edits.before: `shares`, `shares mut` or `thread_shared` value, a class object, an `Array`, `Map` or `Set`)
edits.after: `shares` or `shares mut` value, a class object, an `Array`, `Map` or `Set`; never the block that holds a `thread_shared` value's header, `[TYP-46]`)
edits.why_general: ALC-1 repeats TYP-46's list, so it gets the same change and the same property, and points to TYP-46 for the reason. The two rules then never disagree. A class object made `thread_shared` is still in the list as a class object. The clause decides its block by the property, not by its spelling.

answers.program:
from std.sync import Atomic
import std.thread

class Stats:
    hits: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)

fn main():
    level = Arena.with_capacity(64 * 1024)               # a one-thread arena
    stats = thread_shared Stats() using level

answers.today: On paper it compiles: TYP-46 (p04 433-434) and ALC-1 (p09 185-186) list `thread_shared` among the types `using` may follow. GRM-43 (p03 435-438) binds `using level` to `Stats()`, a class object made in `level`. A class object "already has its block" when it is made shared (HEAP-3, p09 60-61), so the shared object's block, header included, comes from `level`. OBJ-1 (p08 69-71) reads the making thread only from the header of the memory chunk the block came from, and a block from `level` has no such header. Moving the owner into the task's capture is a hand-over (RC-4 point 4, p08 176-178), so the last owner ends on the task's thread and gives the block back to the one-thread arena there. No rule says how the counts or the end run, so the behaviour is undefined. In C++ terms: a biased reference count reading a garbage owner id, on a `std::allocate_shared` from a one-thread `std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource`.
answers.after: E2114 at `using level` (line 9): "`stats` is shared between threads, so its memory comes from Ember itself, which records the thread that made it; remove `using level`". Written as `stats = thread_shared Stats()`, it compiles and prints done.

So `thread_shared Stats using System` and `thread_shared Stats() using level` are `E2114` too". ALC-1 (p09 185-186) says the same: "never the block that holds a `thread_shared` value's header".

decisions.title: No manager is named for the block that holds a thread_shared value's header
decisions.problem: TYP-46 and ALC-1 allow `using` after `thread_shared`, and GRM-43 with HEAP-3 makes `thread_shared Stats() using level` a shared object whose block, header included, comes from `level`. But the making thread is read only from the header of the memory chunk that block came from (OBJ-1, verdict 101 fix 1), and a manager's block has no such header. The value may also end on any thread (RC-4 points 3 and 4). The compiler cannot work out at compile time which thread made a block, so the choice is between a run-time record, a different counting scheme and a refusal. The refusal must be keyed to that one block, so that a `using` naming a list's buffer or a field's memory on the same line is not caught.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. A keeps every thread_shared value on the measured two-count path. Its cost is the block itself: one runtime allocation and one free per shared object, as C++'s std::make_shared pays one heap allocation. Against std::allocate_shared over a std::pmr::monotonic_buffer_resource, which bumps a pointer, that is one allocation and one free more per object (to measure). B and C instead slow every count of these values: B reads the maker from the object (cross-thread copying 13% to 44% slower, measured), and C uses one atomic count (it loses the measured 25% for a thread's own objects). Shared objects are made far less often than they are counted, so A is the cheaper side. 2. Safety. All three are safe, and A turns undefined behaviour into a refusal at the line. 3. Compile time first. A is decided when compiling. B or C would be needed only if refusing lost a correct program, and none is lost: the object's meaning (shared between threads) stays without `using`, and its lists and fields can still take their memory from any manager, the arena's speed included (the Level and keyword-list siblings). 4. A written word only for meaning. A removes a word that cannot do what it says and adds nothing to write. 5. The ordinary program is unchanged. 6. Consistency. There is one way to find the making thread (OBJ-1, verdict 101 fix 1) and no second header path (checklist 13). The refusal sits at the making line or the type, as verdict 165's does, and a list's buffer is decided by verdict 164 in both of its spellings.
decisions.recommendation: A. It keeps verdict 101's single way to find a shared object's making thread, refuses exactly the one block that needs it at its line, and leaves every other `using` on the line as it is.

owner_short.today: The spec lets a shared object's own memory come from an arena, but the only way it gives to find which thread made the object needs Ember's own memory, so such a program has no defined behaviour.
options: A: refuse naming an allocator for a thread-shared object's own memory, which always comes from Ember itself; what the object holds can still come from any allocator.

B: allow an allocator that has one instance and that any thread may use; the object stores its making thread in its own header (a second way, and reading it from the object measured 13% to 44% slower for cross-thread copying).
C: allow such an allocator; count such an object with one atomic count from birth (a second counting path, slower on its own thread).
owner_short.recommendation: A: one way to find the making thread, the mistake refused at its line, and arenas stay usable for everything the shared object holds.

What changed from the first answer. The refusal is now keyed to the property, "the block that holds a `thread_shared` value's header", and no longer to where `using` stands after the word `thread_shared` on a line. A `using` that names a list's buffer, a field's memory or a function type is no longer caught, and its help no longer leads to E2020. The reason now names the runtime's own blocks ("Ember itself") and not "the built-in manager", so refusing `using Global` follows from it: `Global` is a call to the configured allocator (ALC-2 p09 224-225; HEAP-1 p09 40-42 separates `ember_alloc` from a named manager). outs.notes:
Safety lens: the repaired edit is sound. Every way a `using` can name the block that holds a thread_shared value's header is refused when compiling: a field, parameter or result type; generic code over `A: needs Allocator`; a class object or struct made shared on its making line, a nested making line included; a scoped arena; any manager (an arena, the program's own manager, `System`, `Global`). Each refusal sits at the `using` and its help compiles. Every `using` that names other memory on such a line keeps today's checks. The arena-held mesh compiles, a list buffer in a word-keeping arena is E7015 (164/165), and a reset under it is E3021 (ALC-5). The edit only adds refusals and removes one list entry, so it lets no new program through. No high or medium hole is caused by it.

One low hole: a `using` that reaches a thread_shared type through a type alias. The making line is still stopped clearly, but the place and help of the type-site error are not said.

Re-tests of the first round's refuted/pre_existing holes: S1-4 is still refuted. S1-5, E1-5 and E1-2 are still pre_existing. For E1-2 there is extra evidence: if `thread_shared` may stand before a call's result, even a no-`using` class object would carry a one-thread 8/12-byte header (OBJ-1 p08 63-69, HEAP-3 p09 60-61), so that reading fails without any manager.

Pre-existing, for the list, not filed as holes here:
(a) Repair gap (5) re-read and confirmed. A FoundByAddress manager's value held inside a thread_shared object keeps no word (ALC-1 p09 209-211), so Send (THR-8) sees no sharedref mut link. The pool's `deallocate` may then run on another thread while the making thread allocates from it, which is a data race. Same with and without the edit.
(b) A thread_shared list whose buffer comes from a manager can be made (`thread_shared [..] using System`) but its type cannot be written. GRM-3 applies `using` to the whole `thread_shared Array[String]`, and `thread_shared` takes a base_type with no `using` (p03 167-169). So such a list cannot be a field or parameter. This was already so before the edit, where the type form named the shared block.
(c) Sibling 5's line 6 (`thread_shared Array[String].new_in(frame)`) is E7015 only if a call's result counts as a new value. Otherwise it is E7017, because of E1-2's ambiguity.

Message points for the lead (not safety): the general E2114 text ('has no memory of its own') is untrue for a function value with captured state (CLO-10). That was already so for plain `fn()`. When E2114 and E7015 both apply to one `using` (a word-keeping manager), principle 12 picks E2114, whose fix compiles.

Result: no high or medium hole is caused by this edit. Every program in the answer and its seven sibling cases holds as stated. I checked each one line by line against the part files.

Re-tests of round 1's triage:
- S1-4 (refuted): the refutation is correct. The repaired words have no "always", and the OPT-1 against OBJ-1 frame question is the same without the edit.
- S1-5 and E1-5 (pre_existing): correct. The program has no `using`, and the added "only a block the runtime takes ..." is a necessary condition, not a new claim.
- E1-2 (pre_existing): correct. THR-1 (p11 71-72) makes `thread_shared load_stats(...)` E7017. Under the other reading the edit's property refuses it or the object is moved. No reading with the edit leaves the J5-05 danger. Only the error's place stays open, which is the THR-1/OWN-13 question.

Holes of this edit, all low:
1. The `using Global` reason, read beside TYP-46 p04 435-436.
2. With two `using frame` on one line, "remove `using frame`" can be followed the wrong way, into E2020.
3. A `using` brought under `thread_shared` by a transparent alias (or a generic argument) is reached by the property, but the edit does not say where it is refused or what the help says. The two helps can loop: E2114 says remove it, E2020 says add it back.

Pre-existing, for the list:
- The type of a shared list whose buffer is in a manager has no plain spelling. GRM-3 binds a type's `using` to the whole type, while GRM-43 binds a making line's `using` to the value. Only a transparent alias spells it. `owns` has the same asymmetry.
- Whether a manager type name (`using System`, `using Global`) is a legal making-line spelling is unstated. TYP-46 p04 439-440 says a one-instance manager "needs none there". The Parser and AssetCache siblings and the `using Global` test depend on it.
- The general E2114 message ("has no memory of its own") is untrue for a function value with state (CLO-10 p06 276-278). This is the same for `fn()` and `thread_shared fn()`.

Follow-ups outside the allowed rules: E2114's row in p17a line 83 and p17 line 641 need this reason. The repair's notes already say so.

Cost: the stated cost is fair and marked "to measure". A cheaper design is not assessed here: the arena's own chunks could record the making thread. It needs owner input because an Arena may move between threads and verdict 107's promise would widen. The repair's notes record it as a later option for the owner, so I do not count it as a hole.

final.intent: J7-01: a connection-pool server. Its main loop lists the free connection ids under the pool's lock while a worker finishes a batch, and each connection gives its id back to the pool when it is destroyed. J7-02: a game loads textures on job workers and frees each texture's GPU memory as soon as main lets go of it.

existing_rule.words: RC-4 point 2 (p08 166-168): "The making thread empties its queue at each of its check points: it adds each value's home count into its away count, and ends the value when the sum is zero. A queued value is ended by nothing else." Point 3 (p08 169-172): "Check points. The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends." Point 5 (p08 179-181): "it is ended at its making thread's next check point." DRP-8 (p07 865-868): "Anything that may end a value whose type has a `drop` ... makes the changes that `drop` makes, wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them." A check point is a place where a queued value may end, so DRP-8 already counts it as a call of that value's drop. Verdict 101 leaves where the check points go to the compiler ("placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends"). The places listed in point 3 are the lead's choice (decisions.md section 6, "the owner may overturn any"), and the lead made it without thinking of this clash.

edits.before: **Check points.** The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends.
edits.after: **Check points.** The compiler places them at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends; the runtime where a thread waits for work or returns to C from its outermost Ember call. Each may end any value queued to its thread, with what it owns, for every rule (`[DRP-8]`), except inside a queued value's `drop` or a place, open in any function under way, where that end may be refused (a lock held, a walk), marked by the code that opens it in a count of the thread's own. Outside them, a thread in one of the waits named, or waiting for work, is woken by a value put in its queue.
edits.why_general: It states one property of every check point. A check point may end any value given back to its thread, together with what that value owns. That end is the thread's own code at that point, for every rule. This includes the rules that compare one thread with another (a scope's tasks and their parent, a join or a scope's end under a lock, the main thread's module variables) and a reload's compare. The one exception is a place the thread has open in any function under way where that end would be refused: a held lock, a walk, a paused generator's walk, a scope block. A given-back drop already running is the other exception, so ends never nest. The code that opens such a place knows it, so it marks it. Then a check point anywhere under it ends nothing, a library's check point included, and the library needs to know nothing of the program. The runtime adds only places where the thread has nothing in progress (its wait for work, its return to C). It wakes only waits it performs itself, never a call into C or a read. No type, lock kind or construct is named. So with nothing added it decides Lock with guarded by, Mutex, RwLock, channels, scopes, joins, sleeps, generators, callbacks, spawned threads, job workers and C threads. The thread's end is never inside a place, which keeps verdict 101's 'always before the thread ends'.

answers.question: J7-01
answers.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: a free list behind a lock (std::mutex + std::vector)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # one connection
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # gives its id back to the pool
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object, handed to the worker whole
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])   # the Conn is made on main
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the Conn travels inside b; the worker ends its last owner
    for frame in 0..1000:                     # the server's main loop
        with pool.lock:                       # main holds the pool's lock
            for id in pool.free:              # this walk's back edge is a check point: Conn's drop may run HERE
                println(id)                   # ... and would wait for the lock main holds, and push to the walked list
    println(h.join())
answers.today: Two readings, and both are bad. First reading, with DRP-8 (p07-ownership.md 865-868, 'wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them'): the inner walk's back edge is a check point where main may end a queued Conn (RC-4 points 2-3, p08-classes.md 166-171). So it counts as a call of Conn's drop, which takes a Pool's lock inside `with pool.lock:`. That is E7018 by THR-19 (p11-concurrency.md 267-274), at a line that holds no call to move: a correct program refused for a point the compiler chose. Second reading, without DRP-8 (the finder's): it compiles, and main freezes at the first inner back edge after the worker ends b. In C++ terms that is m.lock(); m.lock(); on one thread, with a push into the vector a range-for is walking right behind it.
answers.after: Compiles. Ending a given-back Conn inside `with pool.lock:` would be refused, because its drop takes a Pool's lock. So the compiler marks that block in main's count. No check point under it ends anything, whether in main (the inner walk's) or in any function main calls there. Conn's drop runs at main's next check point outside the block: the outer loop's back edge, or the one before the wait for `pool.lock`. It takes the lock and pushes 1. Frames after that print 1, and `h.join()` prints 1. If the worker ends b only after the last frame, the drop runs at the check point before `h.join()`, or main is woken there while it waits.

answers.question: J7-02
answers.program:
import std.jobs

class Texture:                            # a GPU texture a worker loaded
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println("texture", this.id, "freed")   # in an engine: hand the GPU memory back

class Bundle:                             # a plain object, combined into main's list
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load_all(ids: Span[int]) -> Array[Bundle]:
    out: Array[Bundle] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for id in ids:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of id: out.push(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=id)])))   # each Texture is made on a worker
    return out

fn render_frame(n: int):
    println("frame", n)

fn main():
    bundles = load_all([1, 2])
    bundles.clear()                       # main ends the last owners: each Texture goes back to the worker that made it
    frame = 0
    while true:                           # the game runs on; the workers wait for work and run no Ember code
        render_frame(frame)
        frame += 1
answers.today: Compiles. After `bundles.clear()` each Texture waits in its worker's queue. The idle workers wait inside the runtime and reach no check point: RC-4 point 3 (p08-classes.md 169-171) places check points only in compiled code and at the thread's end. A pool worker ends only with the process, and there THR-16 (p11-concurrency.md 206-207) runs no drop. So 'texture 1 freed' and 'texture 2 freed' are never printed, and the GPU memory stays held for the life of the process.
answers.after: Compiles. Each worker waits for work at the runtime's check point with nothing open. When main puts that worker's Texture in its queue, the worker wakes, runs the drop and waits again. So the workers print 'texture 1 freed' and 'texture 2 freed' soon after `bundles.clear()`, among the first frames, in either order. The drop runs on the worker, beside main, and it only prints, which any thread may do. A drop that changed one of main's module variables would be refused when compiling, as for any other thread.

Each may end any value queued to its thread, with what it owns, for every rule ([DRP-8]) ...' and 'Outside them, a thread in one of the waits named, or waiting for work, is woken by a value put in its queue.'

sibling_cases.case: A server with a Mutex instead of a Lock: a given-back Socket's drop takes the mutex the thread holds while it walks the guarded list.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Mutex

class Hub:                                    # closed session ids (std::mutex + std::vector)
    closed: Mutex[Array[int]] = Mutex([])

class Socket:
    id: int
    hub: thread_shared Hub
    fn drop():                                # records its id as closed
        with g = this.hub.closed.lock():
            g.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Accepted:                               # a plain batch handed to the worker whole
    socks: Array[thread_shared Socket] = []

fn main():
    hub = thread_shared Hub()
    a = Accepted(socks=[thread_shared Socket(id=7, hub=thread_shared hub)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns a: a.socks.len())
    for tick in 0..100:
        with g = hub.closed.lock():
            for id in g:
                println("closed", id)
    println(h.join())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Ending a given-back Socket inside `with g = hub.closed.lock():` would be refused, because its drop takes a Hub's mutex. So that block is marked, and no check point under it ends anything. Socket 7's drop runs at the next outer back edge, or at the check point before the wait for the mutex. Later ticks print 'closed 7', and `h.join()` prints 1. Under today's words the program is refused at the inner walk (E7018), or it freezes.

sibling_cases.case: A renderer with an RwLock: the loop walks under a read guard, and a given-back Mesh's drop asks for the write lock.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import RwLock

class Assets:                                 # names of freed meshes (std::shared_mutex + std::vector)
    freed: RwLock[Array[String]] = RwLock([])

class Mesh:
    name: String
    assets: thread_shared Assets
    fn drop():
        with w = this.assets.freed.write():
            w.push(owns copy of this.name)

class Chunk:                                  # a plain chunk handed to a loader thread whole
    meshes: Array[thread_shared Mesh] = []

fn main():
    assets = thread_shared Assets()
    c = Chunk(meshes=[thread_shared Mesh(name=String("rock"), assets=thread_shared assets)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns c: c.meshes.len())
    for frame in 0..100:
        with r = assets.freed.read():
            for n in r:
                println(n)
    println(h.join())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Inside the read block, a given-back Mesh's drop would wait for a write lock that this thread's own read guard blocks. Its end there would be refused, so the block is marked. The drop runs at the next outer back edge. Later frames print 'rock', and `h.join()` prints 1.

sibling_cases.case: A physics step where the given-back value's drop touches only an Atomic: the same words leave the lock block unmarked and keep the inner walk's check point.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Atomic, Lock

class World:
    live: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    names: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

class Body:
    world: thread_shared World
    fn drop():                                # one body fewer
        this.world.live.fetch_sub(1)

class Island:                                 # a plain island handed to a solver thread whole
    bodies: Array[thread_shared Body] = []

fn main():
    world = thread_shared World()
    world.live.fetch_add(1)
    isl = Island(bodies=[thread_shared Body(world=thread_shared world)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns isl: isl.bodies.len())
    for step in 0..100:
        with world.lock:
            for n in world.names:
                println(n)
        println(world.live.load())
    println(h.join())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Body's drop takes no lock and changes no walked list, so its end is allowed everywhere. Nothing is marked and no count is touched. Check points stay at every back edge, the inner walk under `world.lock` included. `live` drops to 0 at main's first check point after the solver ends `isl`, so later steps print 0.

sibling_cases.case: A network thread blocked in a channel receive, not a job worker: a buffer goes back to it while it waits.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Receiver, Sender, channel

class Buffer:                                 # a pooled network buffer
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println("buffer", this.id, "returned")

class Request:                                # a plain object; its buffers travel inside it
    bufs: Array[thread_shared Buffer] = []

fn net(tx: Sender[Request], stop: Receiver[int]):
    tx.send(owns Request(bufs=[thread_shared Buffer(id=1)])).expect("main is gone")
    if stop.recv() exists as c:               # the network thread now waits for a stop command
        println("stop", c)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Request](capacity=8)
    stop_tx, stop_rx = channel[int](capacity=1)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx, owns stop_rx: net(tx, stop_rx))
    if rx.recv() exists as req:
        println(req.bufs.len())              # req ends with this block: Buffer 1 goes back to the network thread
    for frame in 0..1000:
        println("frame", frame)
    stop_tx.send(owns 0).expect("net is gone")
    h.join()
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. The network thread waits in `stop.recv()`, a channel receive, with nothing open. Main putting Buffer 1 in its queue wakes it. It prints 'buffer 1 returned' among the first frames and waits again. Under today's words the line comes only after main sends stop, after 1000 frames, because the thread's next check point is its end.

sibling_cases.case: A game's HUD counts GPU memory in a module variable that a Texture's drop lowers; the Texture is made in a job and given back to that job's worker.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.jobs
from std.sync import Atomic

static GPU_BYTES: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)     # GPU memory in use, shown on the HUD

class Texture:                                # a GPU texture a worker loaded
    id: int
    bytes: int
    fn drop():
        GPU_BYTES.fetch_sub(this.bytes)       # hand the memory back and count it

class Bundle:                                 # a plain object, combined into main's list
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load_all(ids: Span[int]) -> Array[Bundle]:
    out: Array[Bundle] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for id in ids:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of id: out.push(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=id, bytes=4096)])))
    return out

fn main():
    GPU_BYTES.store(8192)
    bundles = load_all([1, 2])
    bundles.clear()                           # each Texture goes back to the worker that made it
    for frame in 0..600:
        println("frame", frame, "gpu bytes", GPU_BYTES.load())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Each worker waits for work with nothing open, is woken, and runs its Texture's drop. The HUD shows 0 within the first frames. A breaker wrote the same game with `static mut GPU_BYTES: int` and `GPU_BYTES -= this.bytes`. That version is refused when compiling (E7012). The drop changes a module variable of the main thread, and a Texture made in a job is ended on that job's worker, beside main. Today that version compiles and never frees; with the first answer it raced.

readability.verdict: The text is identical and compiles before and after; nothing is written. Nothing here can be given back, so nothing is marked and nothing runs for it. Check points and marks stay the compiler's and the runtime's, unseen. In programs where a given-back drop would clash, the programmer still writes nothing. The compiler marks its own block instead of refusing a line the programmer never wrote. No program gets longer or harder to read.

final.cost:
J7-01 part, run time, all to measure.
- Each marked place costs one thread-local add when it opens and one when it closes; C pays nothing here.
- A place is marked only where ending a value that may be given back to this thread would be refused, and the compiler knows that from the program. In most programs no thread has such values, so nothing is marked.
- A library marks only its own places that a given-back drop may reach through its functions: its own locks, and walks of what it keeps.
- A check point's normal path is unchanged: one test of the queue. The count is read only when the queue is not empty.

J7-02 part, all to measure.
- Around each wait the runtime performs, one store before and one after, next to its system call. It says the thread is waiting with nothing open.
- On the delayed path only: one load of that mark and, if it is set, one OS wake.
- On a C thread, one test of its queue when its outermost Ember call returns: a thread-local load and compare, like FFI-22's attach check.

C pays none of this, but C has no two counts. A shared_ptr runs its deleter at once wherever the last owner ends and pays one atomic on every count change. Verdict 101's measurements beat that by 25% for a thread's own values.

verdicts_kept.verdict: 43: a call that may take a lock this thread holds is refused when compiling
verdicts_kept.how: Kept. A given-back value is never ended inside a block where its drop would take a lock the thread holds: the block is marked, so nothing waits for a held lock. Ends at check points outside such blocks count for every rule, so a join or a scope's end under a lock, whose thread may end such a value, is still refused when compiling (S1-3's program is E7018, as today). An end the programmer writes under the lock is refused exactly as before. Nothing is checked while running beyond the count that tells a check point it is inside a marked block.

The first answer's 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do' is withdrawn. Inside a marked place no check point ends anything, so there is nothing there to count. Ends the source writes keep verdict 57's refusals unchanged.

verdicts_kept.how: Kept. The two counts are unchanged. The making thread still deletes a given-back value at its next check point. The compiler places the check points, and the runtime adds its wait for work and the return to C. A marked place has none for given-back values. The thread's end is never inside a place, so it always deletes there. A value whose making thread has ended is still deleted at once by the other thread, unchanged. J7-01 C and J7-02 B (count atomically from the start) would give up verdict 101's plain count on the making thread, and are not chosen.

decisions.title: Where the making thread may end a given-back value (J7-01)
decisions.problem: Another thread can end the last owner of a thread_shared value that travelled to it inside another object. The value then goes back to its making thread, which ends it at a check point. Read with DRP-8, a check point inside a `with` block or a walk counts as a call of that value's drop. The same holds for a check point inside a function called there, a library's included. If the drop takes the held lock or changes the walked list, today's words do one of two things. They refuse a correct program at a line it never wrote, or (read without DRP-8) they let it freeze. The first answer placed points by what the callers hold, which code compiled once (a library) cannot know. It also took the ends out of what functions do, which hid them from the rules that compare threads.

#    `Pool` lock this thread holds (line 12); walk a copy after the lock"
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:
            ids = copy of pool.free
        for id in ids:

A helper with a loop, or `n.to_upper()`, called inside the block compiles and ends nothing there. The bound: the first check point after main leaves the block, and always the thread's end.

options.outcome: Compiles. The worker runs Conn's drop and waits for the pool's lock until main's `with` block ends. Every count change of such a type is atomic, on main too. That gives up verdict 101's measured 25% for a thread's own values of those types. This is the same idea as J7-02's B.

It keeps its check point, which ends the Conn under the lock and freezes (m.lock(); m.lock();). Or it has none anywhere, and a thread whose loop is in a library never ends given-back values. And with the ends left out of what functions do, three places stop seeing them: a scope's end under the lock, a task beside its parent, and a reload. The result is a freeze or a race.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. A refuses correct programs (ease). C gives up measured speed and verdict 101's plain count for those types. D cannot be built where a function is compiled once for every caller, so it either freezes there or never ends given-back values in library loops. E puts two adds on every loop of every program. B keeps all three. 2. Safety. Under B a given-back value ends only where its end passes every rule. That includes the rules comparing this thread with other threads, tasks and a reloaded image. It never ends inside something this thread has open, or inside another given-back drop. Nothing waits for a held lock, and nothing changes a walked list. 3. Compile time first. Where to mark is decided when compiling. Only run time knows whether a caller has such a place open while code compiled once is running. One thread-local count is the cheapest way to tell, and it is paid only where a clash is possible. 4. Written word: none. 5. Ordinary program: unchanged. 6. Consistency. Verdict 57 is applied in full: a check point that may end a Conn counts as ending it, for every rule. Verdict 43 holds. Verdict 101's 'next check point, placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends' is kept. The critic's bound is the first check point after the thread leaves the marked place, and always the thread's end, where nothing is open. A thread that holds the clashing lock for its whole loop keeps the value until it lets go. That is the earliest that drop can run without waiting for ever.

owner_short.one_line: A destructor (~Conn()) that another thread gave back to the thread that made the object, run later by that thread: may it run inside that thread's lock_guard block or range-for, or inside a function called from there?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | makes a Conn inside a Batch and hands the batch to a worker | the Conn was made on main |
| 2 | worker | lets go of the last owner of the Conn | the Conn goes back to main |
| 3 | main | walks the pool's free list inside `with pool.lock:` | a loop turn is where main may run given-back destructors |
| 4 | main (today) | would run ~Conn(), which takes the pool's lock and pushes to the walked list | refused at a line the programmer never wrote, or frozen (m.lock(); m.lock();) |
| 5 | compiler (B) | marks the block in a per-thread count; nothing given back is destroyed under it, in main or in anything main calls | compiles; ~Conn() runs at the next loop turn outside; later frames print 1 |
owner_short.today: The text either refuses the program at a line it never wrote, or lets main freeze holding its own lock.
options: A: refuse it; the programmer copies the list out of the lock and walks the copy.

B: compile it; the compiler marks each block where a given-back destructor would clash (one thread-local add in, one out), and nothing given back is destroyed inside it, in any function it calls either.
C: compile it; objects whose destructor reaches outside them are counted atomically from the start, so the worker runs the destructor itself (slower counts for those types).

D: compile it with nothing at run time: no destruction point where it would clash, judged with what the callers hold (needs a copy of each function per caller, impossible for a library compiled once).
E: compile it; every lock block and every loop over a list is marked, whatever the destructors do (two thread-local adds per loop in every program).
owner_short.recommendation: B: nothing to write, nothing correct refused, two thread-local adds only around the blocks that clash; ~Conn() runs at the first point after main lets go.

decisions.title: When a waiting or C-side making thread ends a given-back value (J7-02)
decisions.problem: A value can go back to a making thread that is idle (a job worker waiting for work, a thread blocked in a receive) or is back in C (a host thread). Such a thread reaches no check point, so the value's drop may never run: a pool worker ends only with the process, and there no drop runs. When a value arrives is a run-time fact the compiler cannot know, so only a run-time mechanism remains. The first answer's wake reached every call and every runtime loop: a call into C, a read, a given-back drop's own lock wait, the runtime's half-done work. It also ran the drop on a worker where no rule judged it.

# with nothing open, is woken by a value put in its queue and ends it; a thread inside a call into C is
# never interrupted; an end at a worker's wait is that worker's code, beside main, for every rule
options.outcome: Compiles. The workers print 'texture 1 freed' and 'texture 2 freed' soon after `bundles.clear()`. A drop that changed one of main's module variables would be refused when compiling (E7012), since a worker ends it beside main. A C thread's bound is the return of its next outermost call into Ember.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. C keeps a resource for ever (not robust). B gives up speed and verdict 101's plain count. D puts two atomic steps on every call from C into Ember and changes who deletes. A keeps speed and ease and bounds the wait. 2. Safety. A value ended at a worker's wait or at a return to C is that thread's code there, beside main, judged by every rule. So a drop that changes one of main's module variables is refused when compiling, as it is for any other thread. A thread inside a call into C or an OS read is never interrupted. A thread is never woken from inside a given-back drop, so drops never nest. 3. Run time only where compile time cannot decide (when a value arrives), and then the cheapest way. Nothing is added on the normal path: one store beside each runtime wait, and one load and one wake on the rare delayed path. 4. Written word: none. 5. Ordinary program: unchanged. 6. Consistency. Verdict 101's 'the making thread deletes it at its next check point' is kept, with one queue model for compiled code, the runtime's waits and C threads. The runtime cannot run Ember code while a thread is in C, so a C thread's bound is the return of its next outermost call into Ember. Only D closes that rest, and D is the owner's because it changes who deletes.

owner_short.one_line: A destructor given back to a thread that is idle (a pool worker waiting for work, a thread blocked in recv, or a C thread back in C code): when does it run, and what may it touch there?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | worker | loads a Texture inside a Bundle that goes to main | made on the worker |
| 2 | main | clears the bundles | each Texture goes back to its worker |
| 3 | worker (today) | is idle, waiting for work | ~Texture() never runs; the GPU memory is held until the process ends |
| 4 | runtime (A) | wakes the waiting worker | it runs ~Texture() and waits again |

owner_short.today: A value given back to an idle worker or to a C thread waits until that thread runs Ember code again, which for an idle worker may be never.
options: A: a waiting thread is woken to run what was given back; a C thread runs it when its outermost call into Ember returns; the destructor counts as that thread's code, so one that changes main's globals is refused.
B: objects made on workers or C threads are counted atomically from the start, so whoever lets go last destroys them at once (slower counts).
C: keep today's text: the destructor waits until that thread runs Ember code again, possibly never.
D: while the making thread is blocked or in C, the thread that lets go last destroys the object itself (two atomic steps on every call from C into Ember).
owner_short.recommendation: A: every given-back destructor runs promptly on a waiting thread, the fast counts stay, and the cost falls only on the rare given-back object; a C thread's bound is its next call into Ember.

final.notes:
What the repair changes from the first answer.
- It withdraws 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do'. Ends at check points now count for every rule, as DRP-8 and verdict 57 say, so the rules that compare threads and images see them again.
- It replaces static placement 'judged ... in the calls that lead to it' with a mark set by the code that opens the clashing place. Code compiled once (a library) then needs to know nothing.
- It limits the runtime's points to the wait for work and the return to C, and the wake to the waits the runtime performs.
- It counts what a queued value owns.
- It never empties the queue inside a given-back drop.
The new text is shorter than the first answer's (the script measures).

The three causes:
- A: the ends were taken out of what functions do, so the rules comparing threads and images lost them (S1-1, S1-2, S1-3, E1-2, E1-5, E1-7, E1-8).
- B: the wake and the runtime's points reached waits that cannot be woken and work in progress (E1-1, E1-3, E1-6).
- C: placement was decided from the callers, which separately compiled code cannot know (E1-4).

A consequence the owner should see: a thread_shared value made in a job and given back to that job's worker has its drop run on the worker. So a drop that changes one of main's module variables is now E7012 (STA-1, p05-declarations.md 478-480, applied to that thread). It races with the first answer and leaks with today's text.

Possible objection: EFF-25 (p10 114-115) and BLD-14 (p17 226-228) say a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does. Under B, the drops' bodies decide which places are marked, and so when a given-back value is ended inside the window verdict 101 already leaves to the compiler. Option E (mark every lock and walk by kind) avoids that, at two adds on every walk of every program. It is recorded and not chosen.

Pre-existing gaps for the list, not caused by this edit:
(1) Ember never learns that a host thread has ended (FFI-27; FFI-31a). So verdict 101's 'always before the thread ends' cannot be kept for a C thread.
(2) A drop that blocks on a channel only its own thread receives from can stop that thread (DRP-4 only says SHOULD NOT).
(3) A given-back drop that takes a lock while the thread holds another lock it does not clash with adds a lock order. Ember refuses no two-lock (ABBA) order today.
(4) main's thread-end check point must come before the process ends (THR-16).
(5) New, from S1-4: a check point inside `unsafe` code can run a given-back drop that changes what the unsafe block vouches for (a raw pointer into a list the drop grows). The programmer cannot see the hidden end. Today's text has the same check point.

Process: read-only throughout. Only the Read and Grep tools were used. Nothing was written, run or counted.

triage.evidence: With the edit, the runtime has a check point before a worker's wait for work. The edit says 'A thread blocked in a call right after a check point is woken by a value put in its queue, ends it, and blocks again' (p08 169-171 as edited). 'judged against everything the thread has open there' finds nothing open on an idle worker. So Texture's drop runs `FREED.push` on the worker while main pushes. The edit judges the point only by what the thread has open. STA-1 ('reached only by the main thread and its scoped tasks ... another thread that reaches it otherwise is E7012', p05-declarations.md 478-480) is not part of that judgement. If a reader adds it, the point is left out and the Texture silently leaks. Today p08 169-171 puts no check point in the runtime, and a worker ends only with the process (THR-16, p11 206-207): a leak, no race.

Today two rules put the push into the loader's summary: DRP-8 ('wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them', p07 865-868) and EFF-24 ('from the drop of every object it may end', p10 95-96). The edit's 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do ([EFF-24])' removes it. So THR-11 ('checked against the other tasks and the parent', p11 390-396) no longer refuses the program. The loader has nothing open, so its back edges end Texture 1 while main pushes to FREED in the scope block: a race. On the reading that leaves those points out, the thread end goes too, and 'A queued value is ended by nothing else' (p08 167-168) leaves the value orphaned. Today, on the DRP-8 reading the first answer itself takes, it is E7007.

Today the opener's check points add Conn's drop to its summary: a Pool's lock and pool.free (DRP-8 p07 865-868, EFF-24 p10 95-96). THR-5 then refuses the program: 'A with scope block that ends inside a lock's with block, when a task's function changes what that lock guards, is E7018' (p11 384-386, with THR-19 p11 272-273). Under the edit's 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do', nothing is added and it compiles. Nothing is open on the opener's thread, so its back edge runs Conn's drop. The drop waits for pool.lock, which main holds. Main waits at the scope's end for the opener: the program freezes.

Today p08 169-171 puts a check point at the unsafe loop's back edge. A counting loop may add to the list (BRW-18, p07 527-531). The Voice queued to main while it waited at the scope's end (p08 166-167) is ended at that first back edge. So the write through p into freed memory happens with no edit. The edit removes no check point from unsafe code. This is a new gap for the list.

With the edit, main waits for pool.lock right after its check point and is woken. It ends a Conn, and Conn's drop waits for pool.lock right after the check point before its own `with this.pool.lock:`. Each later arrival wakes it there and nests one more drop, by 'woken by a value put in its queue, ends it, and blocks again' (p08 169-171 as edited). DRP-4 does not refuse a blocking drop ('SHOULD NOT block', p07 849-850). This goes on until RT-12 aborts with 'stack overflow in <function>' (p18-implementation.md 297-304). Today a blocked thread is not woken. The queue is emptied at the check point before checker.join(), after the lock is free, where no drop blocks.

This is S1-1's mechanism with a `static mut int`. The edit's runtime check point before the wait for work, plus its wake (p08 169-171 as edited), runs `GPU_BYTES -= this.bytes` on the worker while main reads GPU_BYTES. The edit judges the point only by what the worker has open, which is nothing. THR-20 (p11 287-290) and STA-1 (p05-declarations.md 478-480) do not judge it. Today no check point is reached on the idle workers, so nothing runs there: a leak, no race.

A `safe fn` with no stated effects has 'every effect when none are stated' (p16-ffi.md 74-75). Block is among them ('a blocking receive or read', p10 14). So a check point comes before getchar (p08 169-171). The edit's wake reaches 'A thread blocked in a call right after a check point'. That promises to run Ember code on a thread inside C's read(). Only a signal could do it: EINTR breaks the C call, or a signal handler runs the drop where println's lock is unsafe. Today nothing is promised there.

The edit says 'judged against everything the thread has open there, in its function or in the calls that lead to it: none is placed where that call would be refused' (p08 169-171 as edited). So the check point in std.string's to_upper depends on its callers' locks and on this program's Conn. But std is generated once as its own package (BLD-1, p17-toolchain.md 213-216), and its build key holds nothing of its callers (BLD-2, p17 217-224). So one of three things happens. The point stays and freezes under pool.lock. Or every library loop loses it. Or a run-time mark is needed, which the words rule out. Today no such promise is made.

The edit's 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do' keeps Item.drop out of run's facts. HR-44 refuses a reload that changes a fact a frame below a checkpoint was checked against (p20-annex-b.md 54-66), and here it finds nothing. HR-3b leaves run's old code running, with its check point at the inner walk (p20 42-53). The new drop then waits there for world.lock, which run holds: a freeze. Today, read with DRP-8 and EFF-24 (p10 96), Item.drop is among run's facts and the reload is E9030.

The edit says 'The compiler places them, and the runtime in its own code: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block' (p08 169-171 as edited). That reaches the runtime's own loops and internal waits: the worker pool's work-stealing queues (p11 495-497) and the C runtime (RT-1, p18 243). A drop that calls jobs.submit there re-enters a half-done queue operation. The edit's judgement looks only at what Ember code has open. Today the runtime has no check points.

The edit judges 'a call of the `drop` of every type whose values may be queued' (p08 169-171 as edited). Conn has no drop. The Lease that ending a Conn ends (DRP-6, p07 854-858) is not itself a queued type. Only the [DRP-8] citation ('Anything that may end a value whose type has a drop', p07 865-866) brings Lease.drop in. On the edit's own words the walk keeps its check point, and Lease.drop waits for pool.lock under it. THR-20 says what is needed in its own words, 'and the drop of everything it owns' (p11 299-300).

Verdict 57 (JOB.md 458-465) says: 'Anything that may end an object ... counts as a call of the object's drop ... a function that may destroy an Enemy says changes LOG'. The edit's 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do ([EFF-24])' makes a function whose check point may end a Conn not change what Conn's drop changes. That narrows the verdict for the compiler's own ends, yet departs_from_verdict was recorded as 'none'.

Conn's drop takes the pool's lock (`with this.pool.lock:`), and the loop holds that lock for its whole life. So no thread could run that drop during the loop without waiting for ever, which is the reason THR-19 refuses such waits ('A wait for a lock this thread holds is refused', p11 267-268). RC-3 sets no latest time for an end, only 'never earlier' (p08 148-149). The program is correct and does what it says. The value is ended at the first check point after the lock is let go, the bound the first answer states against the critic's conflict (inputs 368-372). Nothing goes wrong, so this is not a hole in the edit.

causes.cause: The edit took the ends at check points out of what functions are worked out to do, and judged them only against what the thread itself has open. So every rule that compares this thread with another thread or another image lost them: a scope's tasks against their parent, a join or a scope's end under a lock, the main thread's module variables, a reload's compare. The runtime's new points also ran them on a worker outside any task, where no rule looks. And they counted a queued type's own drop instead of everything its end runs.

The wake and the runtime's check points reached every blocking call and every loop of the runtime. That includes calls into C and OS reads that cannot be woken, runtime operations half done, and a given-back drop's own lock wait, so drops nest without limit.
Where a check point may end something was decided when compiling, from the calls that lead to it, which code compiled once for every caller (a library) cannot know.

tests.name: j7_01_pool_walk_under_lock
tests.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: a free list behind a lock (std::mutex + std::vector)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # one connection
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # gives its id back to the pool
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object, handed to the worker whole
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])   # the Conn is made on main
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the Conn travels inside b; the worker ends its last owner
    for frame in 0..1000:                     # the server's main loop
        with pool.lock:                       # main holds the pool's lock
            for id in pool.free:
                println(id)
    println(h.join())
tests.expected: Compiles, never freezes, ends. Every line printed is 1. The last line, from h.join(), is 1. The emitted code has no queue test inside the `with pool.lock:` block.
tests.rule: RC-4 point 3 as edited (no check point where the given-back drop would be refused); THR-19; BRW-18

static mut SAMPLES: Array[f32] = []            # the mix buffer: a plain std::vector<float>, main's own

class Voice:                                   # one playing voice
    id: int
    fn drop():                                 # a finished voice leaves one silent sample
        SAMPLES.push(owns 0.0)

class Chord:                                   # a plain object; its voices travel inside it
    voices: Array[thread_shared Voice] = []

fn settle(c: Chord) -> int:                    # a scoped task's work; the chord ends with the task
    total = 0
    for i in 0..1000000:
        total += i % 3
    return total + c.voices.len()

fn main():
    for i in 0..1024:
        SAMPLES.push(owns 1.0)
    c = Chord(voices=[thread_shared Voice(id=1)])
    with s = thread.scope():
        s.spawn(owns fn() owns c: settle(c))   # the task ends c when it finishes: Voice 1 goes back to main
    p = SAMPLES.as_mut_ptr()
    n = SAMPLES.len()
    for i in 0..n:                             # a back edge: Voice's drop may grow SAMPLES here
        # SAFETY: p points at the n samples of SAMPLES, and nothing in this loop changes SAMPLES
        unsafe:
            p.add(i).write(0.5)                # after the drop grew SAMPLES, this writes into freed memory
    println(SAMPLES.len())

The Voice is queued to main while main waits at the scope's end. There is no wake today, so main's next check point is the unsafe loop's first back edge (RC-4 point 3, p08 169-171). Voice's drop grows SAMPLES there, and every later write goes through p into the freed buffer.
new_gaps.with_edit: The same. A push to SAMPLES in a counting loop is not refused, so the check point stays inside the unsafe loop. The wake saves this timing only under the narrow reading, where the check point before the scope's end is placed. Under the broad reading it is left out (THR-11), and the program writes freed memory as today.

from std.ffi import ForeignCallback, Retained

class Texture:                                # a GPU texture made on the UI thread
    id: int
    fn drop():

    @ffi(param(cb, callback(retained, user_data=ud), threads(main)), destroys(remove_frame_cb))
    safe fn on_frame(cb: extern "C" fn(*mut void), ud: *mut void)
    safe fn ui_run()                          # the toolkit's main loop (as gtk_main): calls the frame callback, returns when the window closes

The edit's own count already makes a check point at every return to C safe, because places still open in the Ember frames below keep the count raised. So the restriction to 'outermost' buys nothing. edits.before: **Check points.** The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends.
edits.after: **Check points.** The compiler places them, and the runtime in its own code: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep, work), when the thread returns to C with no Ember call left under it, and when the thread ends. A check point counts as a call of the `drop` of every type whose values may be queued to its thread (`[DRP-8]`), judged against everything the thread has open there, in its function or in the calls that lead to it: none is placed where that call would be refused, and none adds to what a function is worked out to do (`[EFF-24]`). A thread blocked in a call right after a check point is woken by a value put in its queue, ends it, and blocks again.
edits.why_general: It states the property behind every check point. A check point is the compiler's own unwritten end of queued values. So it is a call of their drops, judged by every rule that refuses calls (a held lock of any kind, a walk, a paused generator, a live view), wherever the check point sits and whatever the callers have open. The compiler leaves it out where that call would be refused, never the programmer's line. It also makes every place where a thread stops running Ember code a check point that the queue reaches: every blocking wait, the runtime's own waits included, and a return to C with no Ember call left under it. It names no type, lock kind or construct. So with nothing added it covers Lock with guarded by, Mutex, RwLock, channels, scope joins, sleeps, function values, generators, callbacks, spawned threads, job workers and C threads, and any rule that refuses calls later. The thread-end check point is never left out, because nothing is open there. That keeps verdict 101's 'always before the thread ends'.

    if stop.recv() exists as c:               # the network thread now waits for a stop command
        println("stop", c)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Request](capacity=8)
    stop_tx, stop_rx = channel[int](capacity=1)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx, owns stop_rx: net(tx, stop_rx))
    if rx.recv() exists as req:
        println(req.bufs.len())              # req ends with this block: Buffer 1 goes back to the network thread
    for frame in 0..1000:
        println("frame", frame)
    stop_tx.send(owns 0).expect("net is gone")
    h.join()

decisions.title: Where the making thread may end a given-back value (J7-01)
decisions.problem: Another thread can end the last owner of a thread_shared value that travelled to it inside another object. The value then goes back to its making thread, which ends it at a check point. Read with DRP-8, a check point inside a `with` block or a walk counts as a call of that value's drop. If the drop takes the held lock or changes the walked list, today's words either refuse a correct program at a line it never wrote, or (read without DRP-8) let it freeze. The places listed in RC-4 point 3 are the lead's choice, and the lead made it without this clash in view.

Compile time first: B is decided entirely when compiling, adds nothing at run time, and refuses nothing. 4. Written word: none. 5. out.notes:
The reading the finder missed: DRP-8 (p07-ownership.md 865-868, 'wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them') already counts a check point as a call of the drops it may run, and EFF-24 (p10-effects.md 96) adds 'the drop of every object it may end' to the function's summary. So today's text refuses J7-01's program at a point the compiler chose. It does not leave the case open. The edit keeps DRP-8's counting but makes the compiler place its own point where that call passes. It also keeps the check point out of the function's summary, judging it instead with what the callers hold, so callers under a lock are not refused because of it.

On the critic's conflict, J7-01 B's bound is stated: the next check point after the thread lets go of what refused the call, and always at the thread's end, which nothing can block. A thread whose whole loop holds a lock that a given-back drop takes keeps the value until it lets go; that is the earliest that drop can run without a deadlock. J7-01 C and J7-02 B, 'never queued, all counts atomic', are rejected together, for speed and for verdict 101's plain count on the making thread.

Pre-existing gaps for the list, not caused by this edit:
(1) Ember never learns that a host thread has ended (FFI-27 has no per-thread detach; FFI-31a). So verdict 101's 'always before the thread ends' cannot be honoured for a C thread, and A's bound for a C thread is its next call into Ember. Only D would close that rest, and D is the owner's to choose because it changes who deletes.
(2) A drop that blocks on a channel that only its own thread receives from can stop that thread wherever the drop runs. DRP-4 only says a drop SHOULD NOT block.
(3) A given-back drop that takes a lock the thread does not hold, while the thread holds another, adds a lock order just as any written call does. Ember refuses no two-lock (ABBA) order today.
(4) The thread-end check point of `main` must come before the process ends, since THR-16 says no drop runs once main returns. The wording there is the existing text's.
