holes.with_edit: The runtime's new check point before a worker's wait for work is 'judged against everything the thread has open there'. An idle worker has nothing open, so the point is placed. 'A thread blocked in a call right after a check point is woken by a value put in its queue, ends it, and blocks again'. Each worker wakes and runs `FREED.push(...)` on its own thread while main pushes to FREED every frame. That is a data race. Under the broad reading (STA-1's 'another thread that reaches it otherwise is E7012' counted as a refusal), the point is not placed, and the Textures are silently never freed, which is the leak J7-02 was meant to fix. No message names it.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Two threads grow one unguarded Array at once. In C++ terms, two threads call push_back on one std::vector with no lock: a torn length, a buffer freed on one thread while the other writes it, heap corruption. The edit adds a new place where a given-back drop runs: a worker outside any task, which no rule on module variables covers. THR-20 still assumes 'a drop runs where the last owner ends' (p11 296-301), but RC-4 runs a queued drop on the making thread.
holes.rule_lines: Edit (RC-4 point 3 as edited, p08 169-171): 'The compiler places them, and the runtime in its own code: ... (... work) ...', 'judged against everything the thread has open there', 'A thread blocked in a call right after a check point is woken'. STA-1 p05 478-480; THR-20 p11 285-301; XI.5 p11 495-497; THR-16 p11 206-207.
holes.fix_hint: A given-back drop is checked as code of the thread that runs it. At every check point, the runtime's included, it may reach only what that thread may reach: a thread other than main and its scoped tasks never reaches main's module variables.

holes.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel

static mut FREED: Array[int] = []             # ids of freed textures: a plain std::vector, main's own

class Texture:                                # a GPU texture the loader made
    id: int
    fn drop():
        FREED.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Bundle:                                 # a plain object; its textures travel inside it
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load(tx: Sender[Bundle]):                  # runs as a scoped task
    tx.send(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=1)])).expect("main is gone")
    total = 0
    for i in 0..1000000:                      # each back edge is a check point of the loader's thread
        total += i % 7
    println("loaded", total)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Bundle](capacity=1)
    with s = thread.scope():
        s.spawn(owns fn(): load(tx))
        if rx.recv() exists as b:
            println(b.textures.len())         # b ends here: Texture 1 goes back to the loader's thread
        for frame in 0..100000:
            FREED.push(owns frame)            # main grows FREED while the loader runs
    println(FREED.len())
holes.today: Refused, under the reading the answer itself takes for today. Texture values may be queued to the loader's thread: it makes them, and they travel inside a Bundle (RC-4 point 5, p08 179-182). So its back edges and its end are places where a Texture may end. Under DRP-8 (p07 865-868) they count as calls of Texture's drop, and EFF-24 (p10 95-96, 'from the drop of every object it may end') puts 'pushes to FREED' into the task's summary. THR-11 (p11 390-396) checks the task against the parent: both change FREED, which is E7007. Under the reading without DRP-8 it races, as with the edit.
holes.with_edit: 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do ([EFF-24])': the task's summary loses the push, so THR-11 sees no clash and the program compiles. Under the narrow reading, the loader's back edges and its end ('never left out, because nothing is open there', the answer's why_general) are placed. Texture 1's drop then pushes to FREED on the loader's thread while main pushes in the scope block: a data race. Under the broad reading (a call there would be E7007), every point on the loader's thread is left out, its end included. Texture 1 then stays in the queue of a thread that has ended. Nothing ever ends it ('A queued value is ended by nothing else', p08 167-168), which breaks verdict 101's 'always before the thread ends'. Main prints 100000 with no message.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Either two threads push into one std::vector with no lock (heap corruption), or a resource is silently orphaned for the life of the process. The edit takes check points out of what a function is worked out to do, but its 'judged against everything the thread has open there' covers only one thread's own locks, walks and views. It never covers the rules that compare one thread with another: a scope's parent against its tasks, or the threads that may reach a module variable.
holes.rule_lines: Edit (p08 169-171 as edited): 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do ([EFF-24])', 'judged against everything the thread has open there', '... and when the thread ends'. THR-11 p11 387-396; EFF-24 p10 90-97; EFF-25 p10 106-112 ('what tasks and threads change'); DRP-8 p07 865-868; RC-4 point 2 p08 163-168; STA-1 p05 478-480.
holes.fix_hint: A check point's given-back drops stay in what its thread is worked out to do for every rule that compares this thread with another (a scope's parent and its tasks, module variables, joins). Only the tests of this thread's own locks, walks and views are judged in context.

holes.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock, Receiver, Sender, channel

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool (std::mutex + std::vector)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # one connection
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # gives its id back to the pool
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object; its connections travel inside it
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn closer(rx: Receiver[Batch]):               # an unscoped thread that closes the batch it is sent
    if rx.recv() exists as b:
        println("closing", b.conns.len())     # b ends here: Conn 1 goes back to the thread that opened it

fn opener(pool: thread_shared Pool, tx: Sender[Batch]):    # runs as a scoped task
    tx.send(owns Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])).expect("closer is gone")
    total = 0
    for i in 0..1000000:                      # each back edge is a check point of the opener's thread
        total += i % 7
    println("opened", total)

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    tx, rx = channel[Batch](capacity=1)
    c = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns rx: closer(rx))
    with pool.lock:                           # main holds the pool's lock ...
        with s = thread.scope():
            s.spawn(owns fn(): opener(pool, tx))
        println(pool.free.len())              # ... and the scope's end, above, waits for the opener
    c.join()
holes.today: Refused. The opener's back edges and end may end a Conn queued to its thread. By DRP-8 (p07 865-868) and EFF-24 (p10 95-96), its summary takes a Pool's lock and changes Pool.free. THR-5 (p11 384-386) and THR-19 (p11 272-274): 'A with scope block that ends inside a lock's with block, when a task's function changes what that lock guards, is E7018' at the scope's end. THR-20's own counting does not reach a scoped task (p11 287-290).
holes.with_edit: Check points add nothing to the opener's summary, so the scope's end inside `with pool.lock:` compiles. The opener has nothing open, so its points are placed, its end included ('never left out'). When the closer ends b while the opener still loops, Conn 1 goes to the opener's queue. The opener's next back edge runs Conn's drop, which waits for pool.lock. Main holds that lock and waits at the scope's end for the opener, so both wait for ever. Under the reading that leaves the points out because main's scope end would then be refused, Conn 1 is orphaned instead, and its id is never given back.
holes.what_goes_wrong: The program freezes: in C++ terms, `std::lock_guard g(m); { std::jthread t(work); }` where work's ~Conn() locks m. THR-19 promises this is refused when compiling ('each would wait for the other for ever'), verdict 52 says joining such a thread inside the lock is refused, and today it is refused. The verdicts_kept claim for 43, 'nothing ever waits for a held lock', is true on one thread only.
holes.rule_lines: Edit (p08 169-171 as edited): 'none adds to what a function is worked out to do ([EFF-24])', 'judged against everything the thread has open there'; why_general: 'The thread-end check point is never left out, because nothing is open there'. THR-5 p11 384-386; THR-19 p11 267-274; E7018 p17a 220; verdicts 43 and 52 (JOB.md 361-366, 414-419).
holes.fix_hint: A wait for another thread (a join, a scope's end) counts the drops that thread's check points may run, its end's included, as that thread's own changes and locks.

holes.program:
import std.thread

static mut SAMPLES: Array[f32] = []            # the mix buffer: a plain std::vector<float>, main's own

class Voice:                                   # one playing voice
    id: int
    fn drop():                                 # a finished voice leaves one silent sample
        SAMPLES.push(owns 0.0)

class Chord:                                   # a plain object; its voices travel inside it
    voices: Array[thread_shared Voice] = []

fn settle(c: Chord) -> int:                    # a scoped task's work; the chord ends with the task
    total = 0
    for i in 0..1000000:
        total += i % 3
    return total + c.voices.len()

fn main():
    for i in 0..1024:
        SAMPLES.push(owns 1.0)
    c = Chord(voices=[thread_shared Voice(id=1)])
    with s = thread.scope():
        s.spawn(owns fn() owns c: settle(c))   # the task ends c when it finishes: Voice 1 goes back to main
    p = SAMPLES.as_mut_ptr()
    n = SAMPLES.len()
    for i in 0..n:                             # a back edge: Voice's drop may grow SAMPLES here
        # SAFETY: p points at the n samples of SAMPLES, and nothing in this loop changes SAMPLES
        unsafe:
            p.add(i).write(0.5)                # after the drop grew SAMPLES, this writes into freed memory
    println(SAMPLES.len())
holes.today: Compiles: a counting loop may add to SAMPLES (BRW-18 p07 527-531), extracting the pointer is safe (SPN-8 p07 837), and a scoped task may reach main's static (STA-1 p05 478-480). The Voice is queued to main while main waits at the scope's end. There is no wake today, so main's next check point is the unsafe loop's first back edge (RC-4 point 3, p08 169-171). Voice's drop grows SAMPLES there, and every later write goes through p into the freed buffer.
holes.with_edit: The same. A push to SAMPLES in a counting loop is not refused, so the check point stays inside the unsafe loop. The wake saves this timing only under the narrow reading, where the check point before the scope's end is placed. Under the broad reading it is left out (THR-11), and the program writes freed memory as today.
holes.what_goes_wrong: A use of freed memory in unsafe code whose own reasoning was right: the author could not see the compiler's hidden call at the back edge. Rust puts no hidden call in a loop. Not this edit's fault; a new gap for the list.
holes.rule_lines: RC-4 point 3 p08 169-171 (today and as edited); SPN-8 p07 837; UNS rules p09 263-275; BRW-18 p07 527-531.
holes.fix_hint: No hidden call is placed inside unsafe code: wherever the programmer vouches for memory by hand, a check point counts as refused.

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: a free list behind a lock (std::mutex + std::vector)

outs.notes:
Verdict: broken. Two high holes and one medium hole are caused by this edit. All three come from one root. A given-back drop runs on its making thread (RC-4 point 2), but THR-20 still says 'a drop runs where the last owner ends' (p11 296-301). THR-20's list of threads (p11 287-290) also leaves scoped tasks and scoped jobs out. Today, under the DRP-8 reading the answer adopts, a thread's check points carry its queued drops in its summary (EFF-24 p10 95-96). So THR-11, THR-5/THR-19's join test and E7012 see them. The edit takes them out of the summary ('none adds to what a function is worked out to do'). It judges each point only 'against everything the thread has open there', which covers one thread's own locks, walks and views and never one thread against another. It also adds new run points: the runtime's own waits, and the wake.

The edit's words read two ways, and both fail. (a) Only what the thread has open is judged: holes 1 and 2 race, and hole 3 freezes. (b) Every rule is applied: the points on a worker or a scoped task's thread are left out, the thread's end included. Values then sit in a queue nothing ever empties. That breaks verdict 101's 'always before the thread ends' and the answer's own claim that the thread-end point 'is never left out'.

The answer's own programs (J7-01, J7-02, the four siblings, readability) all check out under reading (a).

Not listed as holes:
- A thread that holds the clashing lock for its whole life keeps the value for ever. No design runs that drop without a deadlock, as the answer says.
- A woken idle worker could block in a given-back drop on a lock that main holds while main waits at a jobs.scope end for a job only that worker could run, for example with one worker. Whether a waiting thread runs jobs itself is not specified (XI.5 p11 495-497), so I could not show it under the rules as written.
- Values queued to a host thread that exits are never ended (FFI-27, no detach). The answer already notes this.

Cost and engineering notes, for the other lens:
- The 'one store each' blocked mark needs store-to-load ordering on both sides, the waiter's mark against its queue re-check and the waker's push against its mark load (a full fence or seq_cst exchange). Otherwise a wake-up is lost and the value waits for the next check point. That loses liveness, not safety.
- Waking a thread that is blocked on a lock or channel word needs every blocking primitive built on a per-thread wait object.
- A hand-off lock must not hand the lock to a thread while it runs a drop during a wake.
- 'Blocks again' must mean the wait resumes and re-checks its condition.
- All of the above are to measure.
- EFF-25 (p10 114-115) says a fact from a body never changes what a line does. With the edit, a far caller's `with` block moves the moment a callee's given-back drops run (output order).

Process: I read files only with the Read and Grep tools. No shell was used; nothing was written, built or run.

checked: J7-01 program walked line by line with the edit applied. Confirmed inside one package compiled whole: no check point inside `with pool.lock:` (THR-19 refuses Conn's drop there), the drop runs at the outer back edge or at the check point before the lock wait, and h.join() prints 1. That outcome needs std's own code under the lock (println's internals) to be judged against main's lock, which runs into BLD-1 (hole D).

J7-02 program walked. Confirmed: the push from the jobs is a reduction (THR-21, p11 408-411); the Textures travel inside Bundles, so they are queued; the runtime's check point before the wait for work, with the wake, ends them on the workers. If a Texture's drop reached a module variable of main, the same wake would make a data race (hole B).
Sibling Mutex: confirmed. No check point inside `with g = hub.closed.lock():` (THR-19 refuses re-locking a Hub's mutex), later ticks print 'closed 7', and join prints 1.
Sibling RwLock: confirmed. Write under the thread's own read guard is a call of the held lock and is refused, so no check point is placed in the read block.
Sibling Atomic: confirmed. The drop takes no lock and changes no walked list, so every check point stays, the inner walk under world.lock included, and live reaches 0.
Sibling network thread blocked in recv: confirmed. The wake applies to a runtime wait, so 'buffer 1 returned' prints before stop.
Readability program (Board): confirmed unchanged. board is captured with thread_shared, so it is handed over at once and nothing is queued.
verdicts_kept: 43 kept; 56 and 114 untouched; 101 kept for Ember waits; 57 narrowed for check points but labelled 'departs: none' (hole H).

Cost claims: J7-01's 'none' is refuted at a package's edge (hole D). J7-02's mechanism is incomplete: the blocked mark needs a store-load fence, every runtime wait must be wakeable through a per-thread wait word, and a wake inside C or an OS read is not possible (hole C).

Neighbouring rules read: DRP-4/6/8 (p07 849-873); EFF-1/3/4/24/25/6 (p10); BRW-18/20 (p07); THR-11/16/18/19/20/21 (p11); RC-3/RC-4/WK-3/OBJ-1 (p08); BLD-1/2/14 (p17); HR-3/3a/3b/44 (p20); FFI-22/52 and the default effects of a foreign declaration (p16 74-75); RT-8/10/12 (p18); STD-22/23 (p15); JOB-2 and XI.5 (p11 493-524).

Own programs: nested wake under a contended lock (hole A); a scoped job's Texture whose drop reaches main's static mut (hole B); a thread blocked inside C's getchar (hole C); a std loop (to_upper) under the clashing lock (hole D); hot reload of a drop body (hole E); a given-back drop that re-enters the runtime from its own loops (hole F); a queued value with no drop that owns one with a drop (hole G); a helper with its own loop under the lock (hole H); a lock held across the whole loop (hole I).

Two further programs found nothing new. A big-lock game tick, `while running: with world.lock: update()`, whose given-back Mesh drop takes world.lock: the outer back edge sits outside the lock, so the bound is one frame. A generator walking a guarded list under its lock: a view of a guarded field cannot leave its with block (BRW-20), so the lock is open wherever the generator is paused, and no check point is placed.

import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock, Sender, channel

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: free slots behind a lock
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # ~Conn() { std::lock_guard g(pool.m); pool.free.push_back(id); }
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object, handed to the closer whole
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn health_check(pool: thread_shared Pool, ready: Sender[int]) -> int:
    total = 0
    with pool.lock:                           # holds the pool's lock while it checks every slot
        ready.send(owns 1).expect("main is gone")
        for round in 0..300000000:
            total += round % 7
    return total

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch()
    for i in 0..100000:
        b.conns.push(thread_shared Conn(id=i, pool=thread_shared pool))   # every Conn is made on main
    ready_tx, ready_rx = channel[int](capacity=1)
    checker = thread.spawn(owns fn() thread_shared pool, owns ready_tx: health_check(pool, ready_tx))
    ready_rx.recv()                           # the checker now holds the pool's lock
    closer = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.clear())   # gives the 100,000 Conns back to main
    n = 0
    with pool.lock:                           # main waits here, right after a check point
        n = pool.free.len()
    checker.join()
    closer.join()
    with pool.lock:
        n = pool.free.len()
    println(n)
holes.today: Compiles and runs under both readings. No check point sits inside a block where main holds pool.lock, and the checker's loop runs on a thread no Conn is queued to. Main blocks waiting for pool.lock while the checker holds it. The 100,000 Conns the closer gives back pile up in main's queue (RC-4 point 2, p08-classes.md 163-167), because nothing wakes a blocked thread. After main has had the lock and let it go, the check point before checker.join() ends them one after another, and each drop takes a lock that is free by then. Prints 100000.
holes.with_edit: Main is blocked waiting for pool.lock right after the check point before it. So the first given-back Conn wakes it (p08 169-171 as edited: 'woken by a value put in its queue, ends it, and blocks again'). Main ends that Conn, and the Conn's drop waits for pool.lock too, right after the drop's own check point. The next Conn wakes main inside that wait, and its drop waits again, one level deeper. This repeats once per wake for as long as the checker holds the lock, up to 100,000 nested drops on main's stack. RT-12 (p18-implementation.md 297-304) then aborts the program with 'stack overflow in Conn.drop'.
holes.what_goes_wrong: An ordinary connection-pool server that works today crashes when a burst of connections comes back while a health check holds the pool's lock. In C++ terms, the pending ~Conn() calls run nested inside each other, with no limit. It is the question's own Conn drop, which takes the pool's lock. The wake sentence makes given-back drops nest without bound, once per value that arrives while a drop waits.

import std.jobs

static mut GPU_BYTES: int = 0                 # GPU memory in use, shown on the HUD

class Texture:                                # a GPU texture a worker loaded
    id: int
    bytes: int
    fn drop():
        GPU_BYTES -= this.bytes               # hand the memory back and count it

class Bundle:                                 # a plain object, combined into main's list
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load_all(ids: Span[int]) -> Array[Bundle]:
    out: Array[Bundle] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for id in ids:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of id: out.push(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=id, bytes=4096)])))
    return out

fn main():
    GPU_BYTES = 8192
    bundles = load_all([1, 2])
    bundles.clear()                           # each Texture goes back to the worker that made it
    for frame in 0..600:
        println("frame", frame, "gpu bytes", GPU_BYTES)
holes.today: Compiles. THR-20's E7012 (p11-concurrency.md 285-292) covers functions reachable from thread.spawn, from a job submitted outside a scope, from callbacks and from exports. It does not cover the tasks of a scope main opens, which may reach main's static mut. The job only makes each Texture, and the push is a reduction (THR-21, p11 408-411). THR-20 (p11 293-299, 'A drop runs where the last owner ends') counts the drop on main at bundles.clear(), and main may change GPU_BYTES. While the program runs, each Texture is queued to the worker that made it (OBJ-1, p08 69-70; RC-4 point 2). The idle workers reach no check point, so the drops never run: GPU_BYTES stays 8192 (J7-02's leak), and there is no race.
holes.with_edit: Each idle worker is blocked right after the runtime's check point before its wait for work, and main's hand-back wakes it (p08 169-171 as edited). It runs `GPU_BYTES -= this.bytes` on the worker while main reads GPU_BYTES in println. The judgement looks at what the worker has open there, which is nothing, so the check point stays. If a reader judged it by THR-20 instead, the call would be refused at every check point on that worker outside main's scopes, and the Texture would never be ended. The words do not say which.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Memory safety: an allowed program has a data race on a module variable of the main thread. In C++ terms, an unlocked write and read of a global int from two threads, which is undefined behaviour. RC-4 runs a queued drop on its making thread, at any later time and outside any scope. THR-20 and THR-11 judge it on the thread that ends the last owner, or inside the scope that made the value. The edit's prompt wake turns J7-02's leak into this race. A game that loads every frame races today too, at the workers' next job, so the root is in THR-20, an allowed rule the edit leaves as it is.

    id: int
    fn drop():

It can leave check points out of every function of every other package, so a thread whose loop is inside a library never ends given-back values. Verdict on the edit. Its J7-01 half is a sound property inside one package compiled whole: a check point is the compiler's own end of queued values, judged by every rule that refuses calls, and never placed where that call would be refused. Every program in answers and sibling_cases does what the answer says under that reading. Where it breaks:

BLD-1, BLD-2, BLD-14, EFF-4 and HR-44 neither generate code against those facts nor compare them (holes D and E). The answer's claim that the J7-01 half costs nothing holds only for a whole-program build.
- The J7-02 half's wake sentence has two high faults. It nests given-back drops without bound under a contended lock (hole A: a stack-overflow abort in a server that runs today). It also makes a queued drop of a value a scoped job made run promptly on the worker, where THR-20 never checked it (hole B: a data race on a static mut of main).
- The wake promise cannot be kept for a thread blocked inside C or in an OS read (hole C).

Not filed as holes:
- (a) Cost mechanism, to measure. The blocked mark needs a store-load fence, not just 'one store', or a value queued between the check point and the sleep is missed. Every runtime wait must also park on a per-thread word so that an enqueue can wake it, because a futex wait on a lock word cannot be aimed at one thread. Both are small next to a system call, but the answer does not state them.
- (b) Waking a sleep: whether 'blocks again' sleeps for the time left or for the whole time again is not said, which matters for frame pacing. Low.
- (c) The new check point at a return to C runs given-back drops while C's frames, and any lock C holds, are still below. A drop that calls back into that C library can deadlock inside C. Today's check points inside callbacks carry the same risk, so it is pre-existing.

Pre-existing root behind hole B: THR-20 judges a drop on the thread that ends the last owner, while RC-4 runs a queued drop on its making thread. So a game that loads textures every frame races today as well, at the workers' next job. The edit's wake only makes the race happen promptly in a program that today just leaks.

existing_rule.words: RC-4 point 2 (p08 166-168): "The making thread empties its queue at each of its check points: it adds each value's home count into its away count, and ends the value when the sum is zero. A queued value is ended by nothing else." Point 3 (p08 169-172): "Check points. The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends." Point 5 (p08 179-181): "it is ended at its making thread's next check point." DRP-8 (p07 865-868): "Anything that may end a value whose type has a `drop` ... makes the changes that `drop` makes, wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them." A check point is a place where a queued value may end, so DRP-8 already counts it as a call of that value's drop. Verdict 101 leaves where the check points go to the compiler ("placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends"). The places listed in point 3 are the lead's choice (decisions.md section 6, "the owner may overturn any"), and the lead made it without thinking of this clash.

edits.before: **Check points.** The compiler places them: at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends.
edits.after: **Check points.** The compiler places them at every loop's back edge, before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, `join`, a channel's receive, a sleep) and when the thread ends; the runtime where a thread waits for work or returns to C from its outermost Ember call. Each may end any value queued to its thread, with what it owns, for every rule (`[DRP-8]`), except inside a queued value's `drop` or a place, open in any function under way, where that end may be refused (a lock held, a walk), marked by the code that opens it in a count of the thread's own. Outside them, a thread in one of the waits named, or waiting for work, is woken by a value put in its queue.
edits.why_general: It states one property of every check point. A check point may end any value given back to its thread, together with what that value owns. That end is the thread's own code at that point, for every rule. This includes the rules that compare one thread with another (a scope's tasks and their parent, a join or a scope's end under a lock, the main thread's module variables) and a reload's compare. The one exception is a place the thread has open in any function under way where that end would be refused: a held lock, a walk, a paused generator's walk, a scope block. A given-back drop already running is the other exception, so ends never nest. The code that opens such a place knows it, so it marks it. Then a check point anywhere under it ends nothing, a library's check point included, and the library needs to know nothing of the program. The runtime adds only places where the thread has nothing in progress (its wait for work, its return to C). It wakes only waits it performs itself, never a call into C or a read. No type, lock kind or construct is named. So with nothing added it decides Lock with guarded by, Mutex, RwLock, channels, scopes, joins, sleeps, generators, callbacks, spawned threads, job workers and C threads. The thread's end is never inside a place, which keeps verdict 101's 'always before the thread ends'.

answers.question: J7-01
answers.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: a free list behind a lock (std::mutex + std::vector)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # one connection
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # gives its id back to the pool
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object, handed to the worker whole
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])   # the Conn is made on main
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())   # the Conn travels inside b; the worker ends its last owner
    for frame in 0..1000:                     # the server's main loop
        with pool.lock:                       # main holds the pool's lock
            for id in pool.free:              # this walk's back edge is a check point: Conn's drop may run HERE
                println(id)                   # ... and would wait for the lock main holds, and push to the walked list
    println(h.join())
answers.today: Two readings, and both are bad. First reading, with DRP-8 (p07-ownership.md 865-868, 'wherever a value of its type may end, for every rule that needs them'): the inner walk's back edge is a check point where main may end a queued Conn (RC-4 points 2-3, p08-classes.md 166-171). So it counts as a call of Conn's drop, which takes a Pool's lock inside `with pool.lock:`. That is E7018 by THR-19 (p11-concurrency.md 267-274), at a line that holds no call to move: a correct program refused for a point the compiler chose. Second reading, without DRP-8 (the finder's): it compiles, and main freezes at the first inner back edge after the worker ends b. In C++ terms that is m.lock(); m.lock(); on one thread, with a push into the vector a range-for is walking right behind it.
answers.after: Compiles. Ending a given-back Conn inside `with pool.lock:` would be refused, because its drop takes a Pool's lock. So the compiler marks that block in main's count. No check point under it ends anything, whether in main (the inner walk's) or in any function main calls there. Conn's drop runs at main's next check point outside the block: the outer loop's back edge, or the one before the wait for `pool.lock`. It takes the lock and pushes 1. Frames after that print 1, and `h.join()` prints 1. If the worker ends b only after the last frame, the drop runs at the check point before `h.join()`, or main is woken there while it waits.
answers.decides: p08-classes.md 169-171 as edited: 'Each may end any value queued to its thread, with what it owns, for every rule ([DRP-8]), except inside ... a place, open in any function under way, where that end may be refused (a lock held, a walk), marked by the code that opens it in a count of the thread's own.'

answers.question: J7-02
answers.program:
import std.jobs

class Texture:                            # a GPU texture a worker loaded
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println("texture", this.id, "freed")   # in an engine: hand the GPU memory back

class Bundle:                             # a plain object, combined into main's list
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load_all(ids: Span[int]) -> Array[Bundle]:
    out: Array[Bundle] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for id in ids:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of id: out.push(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=id)])))   # each Texture is made on a worker
    return out

fn render_frame(n: int):
    println("frame", n)

fn main():
    bundles = load_all([1, 2])
    bundles.clear()                       # main ends the last owners: each Texture goes back to the worker that made it
    frame = 0
    while true:                           # the game runs on; the workers wait for work and run no Ember code
        render_frame(frame)
        frame += 1
answers.today: Compiles. After `bundles.clear()` each Texture waits in its worker's queue. The idle workers wait inside the runtime and reach no check point: RC-4 point 3 (p08-classes.md 169-171) places check points only in compiled code and at the thread's end. A pool worker ends only with the process, and there THR-16 (p11-concurrency.md 206-207) runs no drop. So 'texture 1 freed' and 'texture 2 freed' are never printed, and the GPU memory stays held for the life of the process.
answers.after: Compiles. Each worker waits for work at the runtime's check point with nothing open. When main puts that worker's Texture in its queue, the worker wakes, runs the drop and waits again. So the workers print 'texture 1 freed' and 'texture 2 freed' soon after `bundles.clear()`, among the first frames, in either order. The drop runs on the worker, beside main, and it only prints, which any thread may do. A drop that changed one of main's module variables would be refused when compiling, as for any other thread.

sibling_cases.case: A server with a Mutex instead of a Lock: a given-back Socket's drop takes the mutex the thread holds while it walks the guarded list.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Mutex

class Hub:                                    # closed session ids (std::mutex + std::vector)
    closed: Mutex[Array[int]] = Mutex([])

class Socket:
    id: int
    hub: thread_shared Hub
    fn drop():                                # records its id as closed
        with g = this.hub.closed.lock():
            g.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Accepted:                               # a plain batch handed to the worker whole
    socks: Array[thread_shared Socket] = []

fn main():
    hub = thread_shared Hub()
    a = Accepted(socks=[thread_shared Socket(id=7, hub=thread_shared hub)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns a: a.socks.len())
    for tick in 0..100:
        with g = hub.closed.lock():
            for id in g:
                println("closed", id)
    println(h.join())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Ending a given-back Socket inside `with g = hub.closed.lock():` would be refused, because its drop takes a Hub's mutex. So that block is marked, and no check point under it ends anything. Socket 7's drop runs at the next outer back edge, or at the check point before the wait for the mutex. Later ticks print 'closed 7', and `h.join()` prints 1. Under today's words the program is refused at the inner walk (E7018), or it freezes.

sibling_cases.case: A renderer with an RwLock: the loop walks under a read guard, and a given-back Mesh's drop asks for the write lock.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import RwLock

class Assets:                                 # names of freed meshes (std::shared_mutex + std::vector)
    freed: RwLock[Array[String]] = RwLock([])

class Mesh:
    name: String
    assets: thread_shared Assets
    fn drop():
        with w = this.assets.freed.write():
            w.push(owns copy of this.name)

class Chunk:                                  # a plain chunk handed to a loader thread whole
    meshes: Array[thread_shared Mesh] = []

fn main():
    assets = thread_shared Assets()
    c = Chunk(meshes=[thread_shared Mesh(name=String("rock"), assets=thread_shared assets)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns c: c.meshes.len())
    for frame in 0..100:
        with r = assets.freed.read():
            for n in r:
                println(n)
    println(h.join())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Inside the read block, a given-back Mesh's drop would wait for a write lock that this thread's own read guard blocks. Its end there would be refused, so the block is marked. The drop runs at the next outer back edge. Later frames print 'rock', and `h.join()` prints 1.

sibling_cases.case: A physics step where the given-back value's drop touches only an Atomic: the same words leave the lock block unmarked and keep the inner walk's check point.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Atomic, Lock

class World:
    live: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    names: Array[String] guarded by lock = []

class Body:
    world: thread_shared World
    fn drop():                                # one body fewer
        this.world.live.fetch_sub(1)

class Island:                                 # a plain island handed to a solver thread whole
    bodies: Array[thread_shared Body] = []

fn main():
    world = thread_shared World()
    world.live.fetch_add(1)
    isl = Island(bodies=[thread_shared Body(world=thread_shared world)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns isl: isl.bodies.len())
    for step in 0..100:
        with world.lock:
            for n in world.names:
                println(n)
        println(world.live.load())
    println(h.join())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Body's drop takes no lock and changes no walked list, so its end is allowed everywhere. Nothing is marked and no count is touched. Check points stay at every back edge, the inner walk under `world.lock` included. `live` drops to 0 at main's first check point after the solver ends `isl`, so later steps print 0.

sibling_cases.case: A network thread blocked in a channel receive, not a job worker: a buffer goes back to it while it waits.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Receiver, Sender, channel

class Buffer:                                 # a pooled network buffer
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println("buffer", this.id, "returned")

class Request:                                # a plain object; its buffers travel inside it
    bufs: Array[thread_shared Buffer] = []

fn net(tx: Sender[Request], stop: Receiver[int]):
    tx.send(owns Request(bufs=[thread_shared Buffer(id=1)])).expect("main is gone")
    if stop.recv() exists as c:               # the network thread now waits for a stop command
        println("stop", c)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Request](capacity=8)
    stop_tx, stop_rx = channel[int](capacity=1)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx, owns stop_rx: net(tx, stop_rx))
    if rx.recv() exists as req:
        println(req.bufs.len())              # req ends with this block: Buffer 1 goes back to the network thread
    for frame in 0..1000:
        println("frame", frame)
    stop_tx.send(owns 0).expect("net is gone")
    h.join()
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. The network thread waits in `stop.recv()`, a channel receive, with nothing open. Main putting Buffer 1 in its queue wakes it. It prints 'buffer 1 returned' among the first frames and waits again. Under today's words the line comes only after main sends stop, after 1000 frames, because the thread's next check point is its end.

sibling_cases.case: A game's HUD counts GPU memory in a module variable that a Texture's drop lowers; the Texture is made in a job and given back to that job's worker.
sibling_cases.program:
import std.jobs
from std.sync import Atomic

static GPU_BYTES: Atomic[int] = Atomic(0)     # GPU memory in use, shown on the HUD

class Texture:                                # a GPU texture a worker loaded
    id: int
    bytes: int
    fn drop():
        GPU_BYTES.fetch_sub(this.bytes)       # hand the memory back and count it

class Bundle:                                 # a plain object, combined into main's list
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load_all(ids: Span[int]) -> Array[Bundle]:
    out: Array[Bundle] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for id in ids:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of id: out.push(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=id, bytes=4096)])))
    return out

fn main():
    GPU_BYTES.store(8192)
    bundles = load_all([1, 2])
    bundles.clear()                           # each Texture goes back to the worker that made it
    for frame in 0..600:
        println("frame", frame, "gpu bytes", GPU_BYTES.load())
sibling_cases.outcome: Compiles. Each worker waits for work with nothing open, is woken, and runs its Texture's drop. The HUD shows 0 within the first frames. A breaker wrote the same game with `static mut GPU_BYTES: int` and `GPU_BYTES -= this.bytes`. That version is refused when compiling (E7012). The drop changes a module variable of the main thread, and a Texture made in a job is ended on that job's worker, beside main. Today that version compiles and never frees; with the first answer it raced.

readability.verdict: The text is identical and compiles before and after; nothing is written. Nothing here can be given back, so nothing is marked and nothing runs for it. Check points and marks stay the compiler's and the runtime's, unseen. In programs where a given-back drop would clash, the programmer still writes nothing. The compiler marks its own block instead of refusing a line the programmer never wrote. No program gets longer or harder to read.

out.cost:
J7-01 part, run time, all to measure.
- Each marked place costs one thread-local add when it opens and one when it closes; C pays nothing here.
- A place is marked only where ending a value that may be given back to this thread would be refused, and the compiler knows that from the program. In most programs no thread has such values, so nothing is marked.
- A library marks only its own places that a given-back drop may reach through its functions: its own locks, and walks of what it keeps.
- A check point's normal path is unchanged: one test of the queue. The count is read only when the queue is not empty.

J7-02 part, all to measure.
- Around each wait the runtime performs, one store before and one after, next to its system call. It says the thread is waiting with nothing open.
- On the delayed path only: one load of that mark and, if it is set, one OS wake.
- On a C thread, one test of its queue when its outermost Ember call returns: a thread-local load and compare, like FFI-22's attach check.

C pays none of this, but C has no two counts. A shared_ptr runs its deleter at once wherever the last owner ends and pays one atomic on every count change. Verdict 101's measurements beat that by 25% for a thread's own values.

decisions.title: Where the making thread may end a given-back value (J7-01)
decisions.problem: Another thread can end the last owner of a thread_shared value that travelled to it inside another object. The value then goes back to its making thread, which ends it at a check point. Read with DRP-8, a check point inside a `with` block or a walk counts as a call of that value's drop. The same holds for a check point inside a function called there, a library's included. If the drop takes the held lock or changes the walked list, today's words do one of two things. They refuse a correct program at a line it never wrote, or (read without DRP-8) they let it freeze. The first answer placed points by what the callers hold, which code compiled once (a library) cannot know. It also took the ends out of what functions do, which hid them from the rules that compare threads.

options.code:
# the program is refused at the inner `for` line (E7018):
#   "this loop's back edge may end a `Conn` another thread let go of, and `Conn`'s drop takes the
#    `Pool` lock this thread holds (line 12); walk a copy after the lock"
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:
            ids = copy of pool.free
        for id in ids:
            println(id)
options.outcome: The original does not compile; the rewrite does. Every loop under such a lock, or call of a function that has a loop, is refused the same way: correct programs refused for a point the compiler chose.

options.code:
# the program, unchanged
# ending a given-back Conn inside `with pool.lock:` would be refused (its drop takes a Pool's lock), so
# the compiler marks the block: one add to a count of main's own as it opens, one as it closes; a check
# point under it, in main or in any function it calls (std's included), ends nothing; the outer back
# edge and the check point before the wait for `pool.lock` end the Conn, counted for every rule
options.outcome: Compiles. Conn's drop runs at the next outer back edge, takes the lock and pushes 1. Later frames print 1, and `h.join()` prints 1. A helper with a loop, or `n.to_upper()`, called inside the block compiles and ends nothing there. The bound: the first check point after main leaves the block, and always the thread's end.

options.code:
# the program, unchanged
# a thread_shared type whose drop reaches outside its own fields is counted for every thread from
# the start (all counts atomic), so the worker runs Conn's drop when it ends b
options.outcome: Compiles. The worker runs Conn's drop and waits for the pool's lock until main's `with` block ends. Every count change of such a type is atomic, on main too. That gives up verdict 101's measured 25% for a thread's own values of those types. This is the same idea as J7-02's B.

options.code:
# the program, unchanged
# (the first answer) no check point is placed where ending a given-back Conn would be refused, judged
# with what the callers hold; nothing runs for it, and check points add nothing to what a function
# is worked out to do
options.outcome: This program compiles. A function compiled once for every caller (std's `to_upper`, called inside the block) has two choices. It keeps its check point, which ends the Conn under the lock and freezes (m.lock(); m.lock();). Or it has none anywhere, and a thread whose loop is in a library never ends given-back values. And with the ends left out of what functions do, three places stop seeing them: a scope's end under the lock, a task beside its parent, and a reload. The result is a freeze or a race.

options.code:
# the program, unchanged
# every `with` block of a lock and every walk is marked, whatever the given-back drops do
options.outcome: Compiles, as B. Every walk and every lock block in every program pays two thread-local adds, also where nothing can be given back. Body's Atomic drop also waits until the block ends.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. A refuses correct programs (ease). C gives up measured speed and verdict 101's plain count for those types. D cannot be built where a function is compiled once for every caller, so it either freezes there or never ends given-back values in library loops. E puts two adds on every loop of every program. B keeps all three. 2. Safety. Under B a given-back value ends only where its end passes every rule. That includes the rules comparing this thread with other threads, tasks and a reloaded image. It never ends inside something this thread has open, or inside another given-back drop. Nothing waits for a held lock, and nothing changes a walked list. 3. Compile time first. Where to mark is decided when compiling. Only run time knows whether a caller has such a place open while code compiled once is running. One thread-local count is the cheapest way to tell, and it is paid only where a clash is possible. 4. Written word: none. 5. Ordinary program: unchanged. 6. Consistency. Verdict 57 is applied in full: a check point that may end a Conn counts as ending it, for every rule. Verdict 43 holds. Verdict 101's 'next check point, placed by the compiler; always before the thread ends' is kept. The critic's bound is the first check point after the thread leaves the marked place, and always the thread's end, where nothing is open. A thread that holds the clashing lock for its whole loop keeps the value until it lets go. That is the earliest that drop can run without waiting for ever.

owner_short.one_line: A destructor (~Conn()) that another thread gave back to the thread that made the object, run later by that thread: may it run inside that thread's lock_guard block or range-for, or inside a function called from there?
owner_short.step_table:
| step | who | what happens | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | main | makes a Conn inside a Batch and hands the batch to a worker | the Conn was made on main |
| 2 | worker | lets go of the last owner of the Conn | the Conn goes back to main |
| 3 | main | walks the pool's free list inside `with pool.lock:` | a loop turn is where main may run given-back destructors |
| 4 | main (today) | would run ~Conn(), which takes the pool's lock and pushes to the walked list | refused at a line the programmer never wrote, or frozen (m.lock(); m.lock();) |
| 5 | compiler (B) | marks the block in a per-thread count; nothing given back is destroyed under it, in main or in anything main calls | compiles; ~Conn() runs at the next loop turn outside; later frames print 1 |
owner_short.today: The text either refuses the program at a line it never wrote, or lets main freeze holding its own lock.
options: A: refuse it; the programmer copies the list out of the lock and walks the copy.

B: compile it; the compiler marks each block where a given-back destructor would clash (one thread-local add in, one out), and nothing given back is destroyed inside it, in any function it calls either.
C: compile it; objects whose destructor reaches outside them are counted atomically from the start, so the worker runs the destructor itself (slower counts for those types).

D: compile it with nothing at run time: no destruction point where it would clash, judged with what the callers hold (needs a copy of each function per caller, impossible for a library compiled once).
E: compile it; every lock block and every loop over a list is marked, whatever the destructors do (two thread-local adds per loop in every program).
owner_short.recommendation: B: nothing to write, nothing correct refused, two thread-local adds only around the blocks that clash; ~Conn() runs at the first point after main lets go.

decisions.title: When a waiting or C-side making thread ends a given-back value (J7-02)
decisions.problem: A value can go back to a making thread that is idle (a job worker waiting for work, a thread blocked in a receive) or is back in C (a host thread). Such a thread reaches no check point, so the value's drop may never run: a pool worker ends only with the process, and there no drop runs. When a value arrives is a run-time fact the compiler cannot know, so only a run-time mechanism remains. The first answer's wake reached every call and every runtime loop: a call into C, a read, a given-back drop's own lock wait, the runtime's half-done work. It also ran the drop on a worker where no rule judged it.

options.code:
# the program, unchanged
# the runtime has a check point where a worker waits for work and where a thread returns to C from its
# outermost Ember call; a thread waiting there, or for a lock, a join, a channel's receive or a sleep,
# with nothing open, is woken by a value put in its queue and ends it; a thread inside a call into C is
# never interrupted; an end at a worker's wait is that worker's code, beside main, for every rule
options.outcome: Compiles. The workers print 'texture 1 freed' and 'texture 2 freed' soon after `bundles.clear()`. A drop that changed one of main's module variables would be refused when compiling (E7012), since a worker ends it beside main. A C thread's bound is the return of its next outermost call into Ember.

options.code:
# the program, unchanged
# a thread_shared value made on a job worker or a C thread is counted for every thread from the
# start (all counts atomic), so whichever thread ends its last owner ends it at once
options.outcome: Compiles. Main prints both lines during `clear()`. Every count change of anything a worker or a C thread makes is atomic. That gives up verdict 101's plain count on the making thread for those threads. This is the same idea as J7-01's C.

options.code: # the program, unchanged; today's text: the drop waits until that thread next runs Ember code
options.outcome: Compiles. While no job is submitted, the textures are never freed: the GPU memory is held for the life of the process.

options.code:
# the program, unchanged
# while the making thread is blocked or back in C, the thread that ends the last owner ends the
# value at once; the making thread, on waking or on every call from C into Ember, first waits for
# such an end to finish (one atomic step in, one out)
options.outcome: Compiles. Main prints both lines during `clear()`, and a C thread's values are ended at once. Every call from C into Ember pays two atomic steps (to measure). The other thread deletes in a case that verdict 101 gives to the making thread.

decisions.parameters_in_order: 1. The three goals at once. C keeps a resource for ever (not robust). B gives up speed and verdict 101's plain count. D puts two atomic steps on every call from C into Ember and changes who deletes. A keeps speed and ease and bounds the wait. 2. Safety. A value ended at a worker's wait or at a return to C is that thread's code there, beside main, judged by every rule. So a drop that changes one of main's module variables is refused when compiling, as it is for any other thread. A thread inside a call into C or an OS read is never interrupted. A thread is never woken from inside a given-back drop, so drops never nest. 3. Run time only where compile time cannot decide (when a value arrives), and then the cheapest way. Nothing is added on the normal path: one store beside each runtime wait, and one load and one wake on the rare delayed path. 4. Written word: none. 5. Ordinary program: unchanged. 6. Consistency. Verdict 101's 'the making thread deletes it at its next check point' is kept, with one queue model for compiled code, the runtime's waits and C threads. The runtime cannot run Ember code while a thread is in C, so a C thread's bound is the return of its next outermost call into Ember. Only D closes that rest, and D is the owner's because it changes who deletes.

owner_short.today: A value given back to an idle worker or to a C thread waits until that thread runs Ember code again, which for an idle worker may be never.
options: A: a waiting thread is woken to run what was given back; a C thread runs it when its outermost call into Ember returns; the destructor counts as that thread's code, so one that changes main's globals is refused.

import std.jobs
import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

static mut ROSTER: Array[String] = []          # player names: main's own list (std::vector<std::string>)

class Badge:                                   # a player's badge, made on main
    name: String
    fn drop():                                 # a dropped badge puts its name back on the roster
        ROSTER.push(owns copy of this.name)

class Award:                                   # a plain object; its badge travels inside it
    badges: Array[thread_shared Badge] = []

class Pool:                                    # a connection pool: free ids behind a lock (std::mutex + std::vector)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                    # one connection, made on main
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                 # gives its id back to the pool
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                   # a plain object; its connections travel inside it
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

gen fn roster() -> Generator[String]:          # walks the roster one name at a time
    for n in ROSTER:                           # a Badge's drop pushes to ROSTER, so this walk is a marked place
        yield copy of n

[I: needs Iterator[Item = String]]
fn print_next(ref mut it: I):                  # prints the next name, if there is one
    if it.next() exists as n:
        println(n)

fn main():
    ROSTER.push(owns String("ann"))
    ROSTER.push(owns String("bo"))
    aw = Award(badges=[thread_shared Badge(name=String("cy"))])
    with s = thread.scope():
        s.spawn(owns fn() owns aw: aw.badges.len())    # the task ends aw: the Badge goes back to main
    g = roster()
    with s = jobs.scope():
        s.submit(owns fn(): print_next(ref mut g))     # a worker starts g: g's walk opens there, and g pauses inside it
    for i in 0..3:
        print_next(ref mut g)                  # main finishes g: g's walk closes here, on main
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())  # that thread ends b: the Conn goes back to main
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:                        # a marked place: main's count should go to 1
            println(pool.free.len())           # println's own loop is a check point
    println(h.join())

    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    batches: Array[Batch] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for i in 0..64:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of i: batches.push(owns Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=i, pool=thread_shared pool)])))   # each Conn is made on a worker
    batches.clear()                           # each Conn goes back to the worker that made it; the idle workers wake to end them
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:                       # main holds the pool's lock ...
            with s = jobs.scope():
                s.submit(owns fn(): pool.served.fetch_add(1))   # ... while it waits for a job that only counts
            println(pool.free.len())
    println(pool.served.load())
holes.today: Compiles and runs. After `batches.clear()`, each Conn waits in the queue of the worker that made it. An idle worker reaches no check point (p08-classes.md 169-172). The counting job has no loop and no blocking call, so no worker runs Conn's drop. THR-19 (p11-concurrency.md 272-274) allows the job scope to end inside `with pool.lock:`, because the job changes only an Atomic, which the lock does not guard. The program prints 0 a thousand times, then 1000. The 64 ids leak (J7-02's problem), but nothing freezes.
holes.with_edit: Compiles: the edited words add no refusal. THR-19 judges a scope's end by what its tasks change. The job's own code has no check point, and a worker's wait for work belongs to no task. Each idle worker is woken by its Conns ('Outside them, a thread ... waiting for work, is woken by a value put in its queue', p08 169-171 as edited) and runs Conn's drop, which waits for pool.lock. Main reaches `with pool.lock:` microseconds after the clear and takes the lock first. It submits the job and waits at the scope's end. Every worker is still inside a given-back drop, waiting for the lock main holds (inside a given-back drop a worker is not woken and ends nothing). No worker is left to run the job, so main never leaves the block. With one worker (logical cores minus one on a two-core machine) the freeze is near certain. With more workers, only the timing decides it.
holes.what_goes_wrong: The server freezes in its first frame. Main holds the pool's lock and waits for a job, while every worker sits in the job queue's way, waiting for that same lock. In C++ terms: a std::lock_guard held across a wait on a thread pool whose threads are all blocked on that mutex. THR-19 promises that such a wait is refused when compiling ('each would wait for the other for ever'), but the worker's new check point slips past it. The answer's verdicts_kept for verdict 43 says 'a join or a scope's end under a lock, whose thread may end such a value, is still refused'. That does not hold for job workers.
holes.rule_lines: RC-4 point 3 as edited, p08-classes.md 169-171 ('the runtime where a thread waits for work'; 'or waiting for work, is woken by a value put in its queue'); THR-19 p11-concurrency.md 267-274 ('the end of a with scope block, whose task changes what the held lock guards'); THR-5 p11 384-386; JOB-2 p11 519-524; XI.5 p11 495-497.
holes.fix_hint: A wait for jobs counts what a worker may run at its wait for work as part of the jobs' own work. So a job scope's end, or jobs.wait, under a lock that a given-back drop takes is refused (E7018), as a thread's join is.

from std.sync import Lock

static MIXER_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut FREE_SLOTS: Array[i32] guarded by MIXER_LOCK = []      # voice slots given back (std::mutex + std::vector)
static PENDING_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut PENDING: Array[Started] guarded by PENDING_LOCK = []   # voices the audio thread started, for the UI

class Voice:                                       # a playing voice, made on the host's audio thread
    slot: i32
    fn drop():                                     # gives its slot back: takes the mixer's lock
        with MIXER_LOCK:
            FREE_SLOTS.push(owns copy of this.slot)

class Started:                                     # a plain object; its voices travel inside it to the UI
    voices: Array[thread_shared Voice] = []

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `audio_start`
@unsafe(export("audio_start", threads=any))
pub extern "C" fn audio_start(slot: i32) -> i32:  # the host's audio thread starts a voice
    with PENDING_LOCK:
        PENDING.push(owns Started(voices=[thread_shared Voice(slot=slot)]))
    return 0

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `audio_render`
@realtime
@unsafe(export("audio_render", threads=any))
pub extern "C" fn audio_render(frames: i32) -> i32:   # the host's audio thread, every block: no lock, no wait
    return frames

# SAFETY: the host defines no other symbol named `ui_frame`
@unsafe(export("ui_frame", threads=main))
pub extern "C" fn ui_frame() -> i32:              # the host's UI thread, every frame
    with PENDING_LOCK:
        PENDING.clear()                           # ends the voices: each goes back to the audio thread
    with MIXER_LOCK:                              # redraws the slot list under the mixer's lock
        for s in FREE_SLOTS:
            println(s)
    return 0

# the C host: its audio thread calls audio_start(3) once, then audio_render(256) every 5 ms;
# its UI thread calls ui_frame() every 16 ms
holes.today: Compiles. A return to C is no check point (p08-classes.md 169-172), and audio_render has no loop and no blocking call, so nothing ever runs there. A Voice given back to the audio thread is ended at the check point before the wait for PENDING_LOCK in the next audio_start, an export with no contract, or it is never ended.
holes.with_edit: The runtime adds a check point 'where a thread ... returns to C from its outermost Ember call' (p08 169-171 as edited). It sits right after audio_render's last line, still inside the call C made. render is called every 5 ms, so the given-back Voices are ended there, and Voice's drop waits for MIXER_LOCK while ui_frame holds it to print the slot list. The words do not say whether that point counts for render's contracts. If it does not, the @realtime promise (no lock, no wait) is broken with no message. If it does, render is E4042 and E4003 for a drop it never names, and no line the programmer can write makes it compile.
holes.what_goes_wrong: The audio thread waits for the UI's lock inside the audio callback. The listener hears a dropout, and the audio thread suffers a priority inversion. In C++ terms, ~Voice() locks the UI's std::mutex inside the CoreAudio render callback. That is exactly what @realtime exists to refuse. The edit's own principle (where the end may be refused, it is not run) stops at the function's last line, while C's call goes on.
holes.rule_lines: RC-4 point 3 as edited, p08-classes.md 169-171; X.2 contracts, p10-effects.md 173-185 (@realtime is @noalloc @nolock @noblock @nopanic(explicit)); EFF-6 p10 187-189; EFF-19 p10 233-236; FFI-33 p16-ffi.md 660-666.
holes.fix_hint: A return to C belongs to the function that returns, for every rule and its contracts included, so it ends nothing where those contracts exclude what a given-back drop does.

holes.program:
import std.thread
from std.sync import Sender, channel

class Frame:                                  # a captured frame, made on the capture thread
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println("frame", this.id, "recycled")

class Packet:                                 # a plain object; its frames travel inside it
    frames: Array[thread_shared Frame] = []

unsafe extern "C":
    safe fn usleep(us: u32) -> i32            # C's sleep; no effects stated

fn capture(tx: Sender[Packet]):
    tx.send(owns Packet(frames=[thread_shared Frame(id=1)])).expect("main is gone")
    r = usleep(2000000)                       # a sleep, inside C: the thread waits two seconds
    println("slept", r)

fn main():
    tx, rx = channel[Packet](capacity=4)
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns tx: capture(tx))
    if rx.recv() exists as p:
        println(p.frames.len())               # p ends: Frame 1 goes back to the capture thread
    h.join()
holes.today: Compiles. Frame 1 goes back to the capture thread while that thread sleeps inside C. No wake is promised, so Frame 1 is ended at the thread's next check point after usleep returns. It prints 1, then `slept 0` and `frame 1 recycled`.
holes.with_edit: The edited text says 'a thread in one of the waits named ... is woken by a value put in its queue' (p08 169-171 as edited), and 'a sleep' is one of the waits named. The text never says that only the runtime's own waits are meant; the answer's why_general says so, but the rule's words do not. A thread inside C's usleep can be woken only by a signal. The signal makes usleep return -1 with EINTR, so C sees its sleep cut short and the program prints `slept -1`.
holes.what_goes_wrong: Either the runtime breaks a C call (a sleep, or a pthread_mutex_lock returning early with EINTR, which much C code does not expect), or the runtime fails to do what the words promise. In C++ terms: pthread_kill sent to another thread's nanosleep to run a destructor there.
holes.rule_lines: RC-4 point 3 as edited, p08-classes.md 169-171 ('before every call that may block the thread (waiting for a lock, join, a channel's receive, a sleep)' and 'a thread in one of the waits named'); p16-ffi.md 74-75 (every effect when none are stated); p10-effects.md 14 (Block includes sleep).
holes.fix_hint: Only the waits the runtime performs itself are woken. A thread inside any call into C ends its given-back values at the first check point after that call returns.

holes.program:
import std.jobs
from std.sync import Lock

static ASSETS_LOCK: Lock = Lock()
static mut FREED_IDS: Array[int] guarded by ASSETS_LOCK = []   # ids of textures whose GPU memory went back

class Texture:                                # a GPU texture a worker loaded
    id: int
    fn drop():                                # records, under the asset lock, that its memory went back
        with ASSETS_LOCK:
            FREED_IDS.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Bundle:                                 # a plain object, combined into main's list
    textures: Array[thread_shared Texture] = []

fn load_all(ids: Span[int]) -> Array[Bundle]:
    out: Array[Bundle] = []
    with s = jobs.scope():
        for id in ids:
            s.submit(owns fn() copy of id: out.push(owns Bundle(textures=[thread_shared Texture(id=id)])))   # each Texture is made on a worker
    return out

fn main():
    ids: Array[int] = []
    for i in 0..256:
        ids.push(owns i)
    bundles = load_all(ids.as_span())         # 256 textures, made across every worker
    bundles.clear()                           # each Texture goes back to the worker that made it
    total = 0
    with ASSETS_LOCK:                         # rebuild the atlas index under the asset lock
        with s = jobs.scope():
            for i in 0..4:
                s.submit(owns fn() copy of i: total += i * i)   # straight-line jobs: no loop, no blocking call
        println(FREED_IDS.len())
    println(total)
holes.today: Compiles and prints 0, then 14. After `bundles.clear()` each Texture waits in its idle worker's queue (RC-4 point 2, p08-classes.md 163-168). A waiting worker reaches no check point (point 3, p08 169-172), and the four atlas jobs have none either (no loop, no call that may block), so no Texture's drop runs. The workers run the four jobs. The textures leak (J7-02's defect), but nothing freezes.
holes.with_edit:
Compiles. The scope's end inside `with ASSETS_LOCK:` is checked against what the scope's tasks change (THR-5 p11 384-386, THR-19 p11 272-273), and the four jobs change only `total`. An end at a worker's wait for work happens in no task, so no rule counts it there.

At run time, `bundles.clear()` wakes every worker that has Textures queued (p08 169-171 as edited: 'the runtime where a thread waits for work'; 'a thread ... waiting for work, is woken by a value put in its queue'). Each worker runs a Texture's drop, and the drop waits for ASSETS_LOCK. Main goes straight to `with ASSETS_LOCK:` and takes the lock first, since the workers must wake before they can ask for it. A worker inside a given-back drop is not woken again, so every worker sits inside `with ASSETS_LOCK:`. The four atlas jobs stay in the queues. Main waits at the scope's end for them while holding the lock the workers wait for.

Result: the program freezes whenever every worker has a Texture queued, which is the usual case with 256 textures spread over the pool. Neither JOB-2 nor THR-5 says the thread at a scope's end runs the scope's jobs itself.
holes.what_goes_wrong: A program that runs today (with a leak) now freezes. THR-19 promises that such mutual waits are refused when compiling ('each would wait for the other for ever'), and that promise fails for waits on the job system. In C++ terms: every pool thread is blocked in a destructor on a std::mutex held by the thread that called pool.wait(), as in `std::lock_guard g(m); pool.wait_all();`. The cause: the new point, a worker's wait for work, belongs to no function of the program, so the rules that judge a wait by what its tasks do never see the ends made there.
holes.rule_lines: RC-4 point 3 as edited (p08-classes.md 169-171): 'the runtime where a thread waits for work', 'Each may end any value queued to its thread ... for every rule', 'Outside them, a thread ... waiting for work, is woken by a value put in its queue'. THR-19 p11-concurrency.md 267-274: 'a join of a thread, or the end of a with scope block, whose task changes what the held lock guards'. THR-5 p11 384-386. JOB-2 p11 519-524. XI.5 p11 495-497. DRP-4 p07-ownership.md 849-850.
holes.fix_hint: An end a worker may make while it waits for work counts, for every rule, as part of every job that worker may run, so a scope's end or a job wait under a lock is judged with it.

import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:                                   # a connection pool: free ids behind a lock (std::mutex + std::vector)
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # one connection, from a networking library
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():                                # version 1 (the library today): println("conn", this.id, "closed")
        with this.pool.lock:                  # version 2 (the library's next release): give the id back
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Batch:                                  # a plain object, handed to the worker whole
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len())
    for frame in 0..1000:
        with pool.lock:                       # what this line does now depends on Conn.drop's body
            for id in pool.free:
                println(id)
            println("frame", frame)
    println(h.join())
holes.today:
Version 1: the drop's body refuses nothing and adds nothing; 'conn 1 closed' may print at the inner walk's back edge, inside the block.

Version 2, read with DRP-8 (p07 865-868): the inner walk's back edge counts as a call of a drop that takes the held lock, so that line is E7018. Read without DRP-8: the same code as version 1, which freezes.

Either way the body decides only whether main compiles. That is what EFF-25 (p10 114-115) and BLD-14 (p17 226-228) require: 'A fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does: it decides only whether a line compiles, or removes a test that would always pass'. It is also the cost the owner accepted in verdict 86 (JOB.md 647-650): 'nothing runs at run time'; 'an edit inside one function (or a library update) can make a far-away line stop compiling'.
holes.with_edit:
Both versions compile. With version 2 the compiler marks main's `with pool.lock:` block: the line now raises and lowers the thread's count (two thread-local adds per frame), and Conn's end moves from inside the block to the next outer back edge. With version 1 the block is left bare, and the Conn may end inside it.

So a library release that changes only Conn.drop's body changes both the code main's own line runs and where main's queued values end, while main's source is unchanged. That is a fact worked out from a body changing what a line does.

The repair names this itself ('Possible objection: EFF-25 ... and BLD-14 ... say a fact worked out from a body never changes what a line does'). It still chooses B and records departs_from_verdict as 'none'. EFF-25 and BLD-14 are not among the rules it may edit, so they still say the opposite.
holes.what_goes_wrong: The specification now says two contrary things, and an implementer must break one of them. Verdict 86's accepted cost (a far edit can stop a line compiling; nothing runs at run time) is widened to 'a far edit can change what a line does at run time', which the owner has never ruled on. In C++ terms: editing a library's ~Conn() changes what your own lock_guard block compiles to.
holes.rule_lines: RC-4 point 3 as edited (p08 169-171): 'a place ... where that end may be refused (a lock held, a walk), marked by the code that opens it'. EFF-25 p10-effects.md 106-115. import std.thread
from std.sync import Lock

class Pool:                                   # free connection ids behind a lock
    lock: Lock = Lock()
    free: Array[int] guarded by lock = []

class Conn:                                   # gives its id back to the pool
    id: int
    pool: thread_shared Pool
    fn drop():
        with this.pool.lock:
            this.pool.free.push(owns copy of this.id)

class Buffer:                                 # a receive buffer; hands its memory back
    id: int
    fn drop():
        println("buffer", this.id, "freed")

class Batch:                                  # a plain object, handed to the worker whole
    conns: Array[thread_shared Conn] = []
    bufs: Array[thread_shared Buffer] = []

fn main():
    pool = thread_shared Pool()
    b = Batch(conns=[thread_shared Conn(id=1, pool=thread_shared pool)], bufs=[thread_shared Buffer(id=1)])
    h = thread.spawn(owns fn() owns b: b.conns.len() + b.bufs.len())
    with pool.lock:                           # the server keeps the pool's lock for its whole loop
        for frame in 0..1000000:
            println(frame, pool.free.len())
    println(h.join())

Compiles. Ending a Conn inside the block would be refused, so the block is marked, and no check point under it ends anything (the answer's B: 'a check point under it ... ends nothing'). So 'buffer 1 freed' waits the whole million frames along with the Conn, although Buffer's drop takes no lock and changes nothing that is being walked. With `while true` it never prints.

The words say the opposite for Buffer. The rule's exception is 'a place ... where that end may be refused', and Buffer's end is not refused there. A single count of the thread's own cannot tell which values an open place refuses, so the words and the mechanism disagree on this program.

That is the 'held for ever' the answer gives as its reason for rejecting J7-02's option C. In C++, a shared_ptr<Buffer>'s deleter would run at once; here an unrelated class's destructor decides when it runs. E1-9's refutation covers the Conn, whose drop cannot run while the lock is held, but not the Buffer.
